articles.title: Watch: US journalist Gershkovich describes being detained by Russian agents
articles.summary: He was arrested in Russia in 2023 and later sentenced to 16 years on espionage charges.
articles.body:
US journalist Evan Gershkovich has told the BBC's Today programme about the 16 months when he was detained in Russia.

In his first UK broadcast interview, the Wall Street Journal correspondent said he realised he had been "lured into a trap" when masked men surrounded him at a restaurant in March 2023, and arrested him.

He was later sentenced to 16 years on espionage charges, but released in 2024 as part of a high-profile prisoner exchange.

He and his employer have always maintained that the charges were false, and following his arrest, then-US President Joe Biden said he had "no higher priority" than bringing Gershkovich home.

articles.summary: Turner’s early 19th century painting - Rome, from Mount Aventine - will be on display in the Italian capital for the first time ahead of an auction in London in December.

A renowned painting by British landscape artist JMW Turner has returned to the city that inspired it nearly two centuries ago.

Rome, from Mount Aventine features a panoramic view of the Italian capital and will be on display at the Palazzo Rondinini for three days.

Dating back to the 19th century, the masterpiece was based on sketches made in Rome.

The work of art is remarkably well preserved and is believed to have never been restored. It even features traces of fingerprints and brush hairs are still visible.

The painting has only been to auction once before, selling for more than £30 million.

Sotheby's now expects it could fetch around £50 million when it goes under the hammer in London this December.

articles.title: Andy Burnham: Northern PM's long journey to power
articles.summary: The former mayor of Greater Manchester has had designs on the top job since 2010 when he first ran to be Labour leader.
articles.body:
Andy Burnham might be a new face at No 10, after ousting Sir Keir Starmer in July, but his rise to power has been decades in the making.

The 56-year-old started out as a special adviser and then an MP in Tony Blair's New Labour government.

He first stood to be Labour leader back in 2010 and then again in 2015, when he came a distant second to Jeremy Corbyn, before turning his back on Westminster and re-inventing himself as the King of the North.

As the first Mayor of Greater Manchester, he built a powerful political brand - affable, down-to-earth and, above all, proudly Northern.

When asked by the website Mumsnet to name his favourite biscuit, the new prime minister replied that he did not have a sweet tooth and preferred "beer and chips and gravy".

Early life: Everton fan and indie music lover

Born in Liverpool in 1970, Burnham grew up in Culcheth, a quiet commuter belt village in Cheshire, near Warrington.

His father, a BT engineer, and his mother, a GP receptionist, were both staunch Labour supporters and he developed an early interest in politics.

Burnham has described how he was inspired to join the Labour Party at the age of 14, after being moved by the BBC TV drama, Boys from the Blackstuff, about life on the dole in Liverpool.

A lifelong Everton fan, his friends remember Burnham as a competitive, sports-mad child, who was a fast bowler for Lancashire schoolboys cricket team.

At school, the local Roman Catholic comprehensive, his English teacher recalls how he stood to be a Labour candidate in mock elections - and won by a landslide.

Burnham credits his working-class Catholic upbringing for having a big impact on his politics, particularly teachings around social justice.

He has described himself as "Catholic by upbringing" although "not particularly religious", but he was sworn in to Parliament over a Bible and will be the UK's first prime minister to enter Downing Street as a Catholic.

While Burnham told the Times his mother would be "wearing her rosary beads out" to mark him becoming prime minister, his father, Roy, will unfortunately be unaware of his son's achievement due to his dementia.

He told The Times: "That's a sadness because he would be (proud). The way I look at it, it's his achievement as well.

"A whole family achievement although he doesn't know it."

Burnham and his two brothers were the first in their family to go to university, with Andy studying English at Cambridge.

In his book, Head North, Burnham wrote that he "struggled to feel part of things" at university and felt like an "imposter".

However, the music-lover - who is a fan of Manchester indie bands like The Smiths and The Stone Roses - said his "growing interest in Manchester music gave me an identity and an advantage".

After graduating, he started out in journalism, working for trade magazines including Tank World and Passenger World Management.

In his early 20s, he got his first break in politics, working as a researcher for the late Tessa Jowell, then MP for Dulwich and West Norwood, who would go on to be a minister under Tony Blair and Gordon Brown.

Burnham rose quickly through the ranks, becoming a special adviser to Culture Secretary Chris Smith before being elected as the MP for his hometown of Leigh, in Greater Manchester, in 2001.

He first served as a junior minister under Blair, but joined the cabinet as chief secretary to the Treasury, and later culture secretary and health secretary, under Brown.

It was as secretary of state for culture, media and sport that Burnham was heckled at a memorial service marking the 20th anniversary of the Hillsborough disaster.

Ninety-seven Liverpool fans were killed in the stadium crush of 1989.

The heckling spurred Burnham on to raise the issue in cabinet, contributing to the launch of a second inquiry into the disaster.

In 2010, after Brown resigned following Labour's general election defeat, Burnham ran to become the party's leader.

He came fourth out of the five contenders, losing to Ed Miliband, but spent the next five years building up his appeal with the party's grassroots.

In 2015 he tried again, beaten this time by Jeremy Corbyn.

Burnham's critics have branded him a weather vane, whose views have blown with the political winds to give him the best chance of success.

He served in Corbyn's shadow cabinet, as shadow home secretary, despite being seen as on the Blairite centre-right of the party.

Burnham's views have moved increasingly to the left, backing the nationalisation of water and energy.

He was not one of those who resigned in protest at Corbyn's leadership in 2016.

Instead he stood down in 2017 to run to be the first mayor of Greater Manchester.

Burnham won the contest with more than 60% of the vote and was re-elected by an even bigger margin in 2021.

As mayor, he has drawn praise for his transformation of the region's transport system.

Under his leadership, Greater Manchester was the first area in England outside London to bring bus services back under public control, while integrating them with other modes of transport under the branding of the "Bee Network".

Other bold pledges included ending rough sleeping in the region by 2020 - although the target was missed.

His profile rose further during the Covid pandemic, when he accused the Conservative government of treating the north of England with "contempt" over regional lockdown restrictions.

The stand-off helped earn him the nickname "King of the North".

By the autumn party conference season of 2025, Burnham was openly on manoeuvres for the top job, as he refused to rule out a leadership bid.

His interventions appeared to backfire, after he provoked a backlash by suggesting the government was "in hock" to the bond markets - a reference to the government's self-imposed rules limiting spending and borrowing.

In January a potential opportunity for a return to Westminster arose when Greater Manchester MP Andrew Gwynne announced he was standing down, triggering a by-election in his Gorton and Denton constituency.

However, Burnham was blocked from standing by Labour's ruling body, with the approval of the prime minister.

By May, the situation had changed. Labour suffered a poor set of election results in England, Scotland and Wales, with Reform riding high in the polls and the party seeing success in Burnham's backyard.

Sir Keir Starmer faced increased pressure over his future, with some MPs calling for change and ministerial resignations taking place.

Josh Simons announced he would step down as Labour MP for Makerfield to make way for Burnham to mount a bid to return to Parliament.

Burnham went on to be selected as the Labour candidate for the constituency and the following month he secured his return to Westminster.

He was then elected unopposed to be leader of the Labour Party and prime minister within weeks.

It might have felt like a seamless transition - but it was a huge political gamble that was not guaranteed to work.

If he had failed to win the Makerfield by-election his political career would have effectively been over - and if all of his potential challengers for the Labour crown had not melted away, he might have ended up as a backbench MP.

Burnham made a confident start as PM, with a blizzard of eyecatching policies aimed at easing cost of living pressures and shifting power out of Westminster.

One of his first acts was to set up No 10 North, in Manchester.

Labour had a modest bounce in the opinion polls, edging in front of Reform UK for the first time in months. This prompted speculation that he might call an early election, which were quicky squashed by the new PM.

But his hands remain tied by the manifesto Labour was elected on in 2024, with little room for manoeuvre on tax and spending.

And although he arrived for Labour's conference in Liverpool in a commanding position in the party, most of the really tough decisions he must take as prime minister - from welfare reform to defence spending - lie ahead of him.

articles.title: Argentina’s Milei seeks to deport foreigners that spread ‘hate’ of country
articles.summary: Experts have cast doubt on legality of the emergency decree as Milei decries a campaign of ‘hostility’ after World Cup.
articles.body:
Argentinian President Javier Milei has signed an emergency decree empowering the government to eject foreigners who spread “hate” about the South American nation.

The legality of the measure, signed on Thursday, has already been questioned by experts. The decree allows the government to bar, deport or revoke the visas of those who express “hate” or tarnish national symbols.

In announcing the measure, Milei’s office addressed the global animus Argentina faced after its appearance in the 2026 FIFA World Cup.

The country reached the final match of the tournament, but its second-place finish was tarnished by accusations of racism among its players and fans. Milei framed that backlash as a campaign to discredit the country.

“In light of recent displays of hostility toward the Argentine Republic and Argentines, the national government reaffirms that the defence of the nation, its citizens and its symbols is non-negotiable,” the president’s office said.

“Anyone who attacks the Argentine Republic is not welcome in our country.”

The decree comes at a time when many Argentinians have expressed frustration over what they see as unfair criticism of their team during the recent World Cup.

That tournament, which concluded on July 19 with Spain defeating Argentina, prompted speculation about favourable officiating for the Argentinian side.

After the final match ended, a brawl appeared to break out on the football pitch. FIFA this week announced it would initiate a disciplinary probe against three Argentinian players and one coach, citing allegations of “unsporting behaviour”. One Spanish player was also cited.

FIFA also said it would investigate incidents of “discriminatory chants and gestures” and “inappropriate messages” from the Argentinian side.

Many Argentinians expressed frustration to see sports fans around the world, including much of Latin America , rally behind Spain, and the allegations of racism prompted heated discourse on social media.

The libertarian Milei has asserted, without evidence, that global criticism is the result of a coordinated “anti-Argentina campaign” financed by leftists in Brazil, Mexico and the United States Democratic Party.

Brazil recalled its ambassador last weekend in response to those accusations and insults directed at the country’s president and members of its judiciary.

Thursday’s presidential decree in Argentina says that it does not apply to ideological disagreement or political, academic or civic criticism protected under Argentina’s constitution.

But it does not include details about how the term “hate” will be defined and whether immigration authorities will search the social media histories of tourists and foreign residents.

articles.title: 'The internet is a strange place': The story of how a small-town 'COVID-conscious lesbian bar' went viral
articles.summary: A Boston Globe story detailing the uproar over the LGBTQ-friendly spot's new mask policy became a major topic for memes and debate.
articles.body:
Mask policies at a lesbian bar in a small western Massachusetts town don't sound like the kind of topic that would become a viral sensation. But that's exactly what happened when the Boston Globe published a look last week into the uproar that ensued when Last Ditch, a bar in the small LGBTQ-friendly town of Greenfield, Mass., decided to transition to a mask-optional policy for its Saturday night happy hours.

"Shocking news … the internet is a strange place, particularly when it comes to extremely niche squabbles," Globe correspondent Dave Beard wrote in reaction to the story's extraordinary reach.

The day after the story was published, the paper's managing editor reportedly told staff that it had generated more than 1,000 new subscriptions, was "by far" the best-performing story of the year and was on pace to "shatter" all sorts of content records.

Online conversation about the "COVID-conscious lesbian bar" ignited with a velocity that's rare even in our viral age. Even members of Congress couldn't help cracking their jokes or launching their critiques.

There are also reports that the ordeal has drawn Hollywood's attention for a potential adaptation.

Here's a breakdown of what happened, why the story became such a phenomenon and the various debates it has triggered.

As told by the Globe, it all started with an Instagram post . On Aug. 31, Last Ditch's management — who founded the bar as a haven for "Dykes, Transexuals, Gender Freaks, Workers, and their friends" — shared a flier with the bold headline "UPDATES!" Among the notices in the post was the line "It is with love we inform our immunocompromised disabled divas we will be opening Saturday nights as mask optional ." The decision was made "after an outpour of feedback from our regulars, volunteers, and team," Last Ditch wrote.

Comments on the post have since been disabled, but according to the Globe, the response was immediate and furious. One commenter accused Last Ditch of "being complicit in a mass disabling event."

"People like you kill disabled people in the name of your own leisure and convenience," wrote another.

Someone else added that they hope the venue gets "firebombed."

The criticism centered around accusations that switching to a mask-optional standard was "ableist" — a word used to describe laws, policies or attitudes that, in the words of the Center for Disability Rights, "devalue and discriminate against people with physical, intellectual, or psychiatric disabilities." According to the Globe, some of the fiercest critics even accused the bar of practicing eugenics , an antiquated and discredited scientific practice aimed at ridding society of those with "less suitable" genetics.

The responses came despite Greenfield reporting zero positive COVID cases since early July, according to state government data.

Last Ditch posted a follow-up two days later that included an apology for the "passive and dismissive tone" used to announce the new mask policy. That did little to quell the anger among the bar's critics, in part because it lacked alt text that would make it accessible to the visually impaired.

The debate boiled over even further during Last Ditch's monthly community meeting the following week. Despite the presence of two mediators who were there to keep the conversation on track and civil, things got heated quickly.

Jackie Matellian, the last of the bar's three founders still involved in daily operations, was bombarded with angry messages from patrons who attended the meeting in person or via Zoom. One particularly critical remote attendee, whom the Globe describes as "a performer and artist who goes by Soe Noire," reportedly flooded the Zoom chat with statements claiming that Matellian was not only disregarding the concerns of disabled people, but also minimizing minority voices.

"I'm hearing a WHITE therapist ... center[ing] the feelings of a majority white and white adjacent staff," wrote Noire, who is Black, according to the Globe.

The 3.5-hour meeting reportedly did little to quell the discontent, but the drama remained a niche story within the small western Massachusetts community until last week, when the Globe published a lengthy feature story on the disagreement.

In its first public comments since the story went viral, Last Ditch shared an Instagram message defending Soe Noire and criticizing the "disorganization of the Globe's article."

Almost immediately, the Globe's portrayal of the fallout over Last Ditch's mask policy became the subject of fascination, debate and jokes across social media.

At first, a lot of the discussion focused on highlighting the many out-of-the-ordinary details from the story — Zoom attendees reportedly arguing that the therapist mediator was essentially a cop, regulars being asked not to approach the discussion from "places of righteousness," the fact that one of the founders stepped back from the bar to attend clown college.

Much of the early reaction could be boiled down to fascination with this deep look into a world that is wildly different from the life of the average American.

"Great article!" one commenter on the Globe's online version of the story wrote. "It reads almost like a visit to another planet, which it kind of is."

The phrase "COVID-conscious lesbian bar" and its variants quickly became cemented in the lexicon of the chronically online, alongside classics like "30-50 feral hogs," "milkshake duck" and "bean dad."

Like many trends that start as a platform for jests and playful memes, the conversation eventually veered into a deeper debate over what the surprisingly enthralling drama at the Last Ditch represents about our society.

Many conservatives framed the story as a prime example of what they view as the absurdity of "wokeness" on the left.

"Leftism is a mental disease," Texas Republican Sen. Ted Cruz wrote on social media.

An opinion piece published by the Washington Post on Sunday carried the headline: "The Great Awokening is over. This lesbian bar shows why."

Some left-leaning critics argued that the virality of the story was entirely rooted in the way it gave conservatives another opportunity to demonize progressives.

"'Woke has gone too far'" outrage bait is very profitable!" tech journalist Taylor Lorenz argued . "This type of content sustains half the internet."

"The coverage was heavily sensationalized," freelance journalist Katelyn Burns wrote on Bluesky. "I think you could go to most local clubs or churches and find people just as wild."

To some commentators on the left, Last Ditch reflects a very real problem of infighting that often happens in progressive communities, which end up battling among themselves rather than promoting their causes out in the broader world.

"The harrowing story is surprisingly relatable … especially for anyone who has spent much time in leftist spaces in the past several decades, LGBTQ+ people who have tried to get more involved in the community, and LGBTQ+ leftists and left-leaning people who want to actually make the world a better place," Alex Bollinger wrote for LGBTQ Nation .

In Greenfield itself, the response has been a combination of bewilderment at the attention their small town has gotten and concern for the future of Last Ditch.

"I worry about their ability to weather this storm," City Council President Lora Wondolowski told the Greenfield Recorder .

A local business owner told the paper she hopes the bar's surprise notoriety will prove to be a blessing.

"I hope it brings them endless business, I hope it fills their doors, I hope it brings business to Greenfield," said Elizabeth DeNeeve. "They're micro-influencers now."

articles.title: Argentina anuncia arbitragem contra Reino Unido sobre Malvinas | G1
articles.standfirst: Gabinete de Javier Milei trava disputa com governo britânico por soberania das ilhas Malvinas, território reivindicado pela Argentina há décadas. Arbitragem utilizará resolução da ONU como base, e presidente argentino ameaçou recorrer ao Tribunal Internacional do Direito do Mar.
articles.summary: Gabinete de Javier Milei trava disputa com governo britânico por soberania das ilhas Malvinas, território reivindicado pela Argentina há décadas. Arbitragem utilizará resolução da ONU como base, e presidente argentino ameaçou recorrer ao Tribunal Internacional do Direito do Mar.
articles.body:
Vista aérea de Port Stanley, nas Ilhas Malvinas/Falklands — Foto: Wikimedia Commons

A Argentina iniciará uma arbitragem internacional contra o Reino Unido por um projeto petrolífero nas proximidades das ilhas Malvinas, cuja soberania é reivindicada por Buenos Aires, anunciou o presidente Javier Milei.

"Determinei à Chancelaria e às nossas equipes jurídicas que iniciem a arbitragem internacional contra o Reino Unido pelo saque ilegal de nossos recursos por meio do projeto Sea Lion, na Bacia das Malvinas Norte", escreveu Milei no X na segunda-feira (28).

🔍 A arbitragem é um tipo de disputa judicial que envolve a busca por um acordo, mediado por um juiz, entre duas partes para prevenir um processo mais alongado na Justiça.

Segundo um comunicado do gabinete de Milei, o país sul-americano se baseará na Convenção da ONU sobre o Direito do Mar na requisição.

"Se em duas semanas o Reino Unido não interromper a exploração ilegítima, vamos recorrer ao Tribunal Internacional do Direito do Mar", acrescentou o presidente argentino.

O projeto Sea Lion, da britânica Rockhopper e da israelense Navitas, prevê iniciar a extração de petróleo em 2028 em águas próximas às ilhas, que são administradas pelo Reino Unido .

A medida ocorre no âmbito da disputa entre Argentina e Reino Unido pela soberania do arquipélago no Atlântico Sul.

As Malvinas, chamadas de Falklands pelos britânicos, são uma questão central da identidade argentina . Em 1982, durante a ditadura militar, a Argentina perdeu uma guerra contra o Reino Unido após tentar recuperar as ilhas.

Nas últimas semanas, Milei retomou a reivindicação de soberania sobre as Malvinas, que Buenos Aires mantém pela via diplomática desde o fim da guerra. Ele disse que tomou a iniciativa estimulado por declarações de seu aliado, o presidente dos EUA, Donald Trump, que não descarta rever a neutralidade de Washington na disputa.

Em setembro, Milei enviou ao Congresso argentino um projeto de lei que endurece as sanções pela exploração de recursos naturais nas ilhas e determinou a retomada da construção de uma base militar na Terra do Fogo, no sul do país.

Na semana passada, o presidente argentino voltou a falar sobre as Malvinas em discurso na Assembleia Geral da ONU, em que chamou o órgão multilateral de "inútil" por uma suposta omissão na resolução da disputa.

Uma juíza argentina havia determinado no domingo a suspensão do projeto petrolífero, atendendo a um pedido de ex-combatentes e advogados ambientalistas. Londres defendeu o direito dos moradores das ilhas de explorar seus recursos naturais e manifestou apoio às empresas envolvidas.

O Reino Unido não reconhece a jurisdição argentina sobre as ilhas, que estão sob controle britânico desde 1833. Há décadas, a ONU reconhece a existência de uma disputa de soberania entre os dois países e insta as partes a não tomarem decisões unilaterais, uma determinação que, segundo Buenos Aires, não está sendo cumprida pelos britânicos.

articles.title: Motociclista ataca mulheres em Guarujá: polícia investiga casos | G1
articles.standfirst: Câmeras registraram abordagens em Guarujá (SP). Duas mulheres, de 21 e 33 anos, relataram os ataques, e a Delegacia de Defesa da Mulher tenta identificar o suspeito.
articles.summary: A Delegacia de Defesa da Mulher investiga ataques de um motociclista contra ciclistas em Guarujá após câmeras registrarem importunação sexual em série.
articles.body:
Um motociclista ainda não identificado é investigado por uma série de importunações sexuais contra mulheres ciclistas em Guarujá , no litoral de São Paulo. Câmeras de monitoramento mostram o suspeito perseguindo as vítimas, apalpando o corpo delas e fugindo em seguida (assista acima ).

Os casos foram registrados por câmeras de segurança em diferentes pontos da cidade e repercutiram nas redes sociais. Nas imagens, o motociclista aparece usando uma bag semelhante às utilizadas por entregadores.

Conforme apurado pela TV Tribuna, afiliada da Globo, os vídeos são analisados pela equipe da Delegacia de Defesa da Mulher (DDM) de Guarujá, que investiga os casos e tenta identificar o suspeito.

Procurada pelo g1 , a Secretaria de Segurança Pública de São Paulo (SSP-SP) não se manifestou até a publicação desta reportagem.

Ataque foi flagrado por câmera de segurança em Guarujá (SP) — Foto: Reprodução

A atendente de farmácia Jéssica Martins , de 33 anos, relatou ter sido vítima do motociclista ao sair do trabalho na noite de 12 de setembro. Uma câmera de segurança registrou o momento em que um homem de moto seguiu a ciclista por uma viela e fugiu logo depois.

Jéssica contou que não desconfiou da aproximação porque acreditou que o homem fosse um entregador trabalhando ou alguma pessoa conhecida.

"Quando eu olhei para trás, o cidadão já veio apertando minha bunda. Nisso que ele apertou, eu já comecei a xingá-lo. Desci da bicicleta, aí perguntei se estava louco, comecei a xingar", relembrou a vítima, em entrevista à TV Tribuna, afiliada da Globo.

De acordo com Jéssica, o motociclista não respondeu e fugiu antes que ela conseguisse anotar a placa. "Fiquei paralisada", afirmou. Depois, ela foi até a casa de um primo para contar o que havia acontecido.

Jéssica e o primo tentaram localizar o motociclista, mas não o encontraram. "Fiquei muito nervosa, com medo, com ansiedade", disse a vítima, que registrou um boletim de ocorrência.

Jovem, de 21 anos, foi atacada duas semanas depois de Jéssica (à dir.) sofrer a importunação. — Foto: Reprodução

Uma jovem de 21 anos, que pediu para não ser identificada, disse ter sido vítima de uma abordagem semelhante duas semanas depois, em 26 de setembro. Segundo ela, o motociclista se aproximou sem dizer nada e tocou o corpo dela.

"Escutei o barulho da moto vindo muito rápido, aí eu fui dar a passagem para ele poder passar. Nisso, eu senti a moto bem próxima, e foi quando eu senti ele me segurando. Ele me segurou muito forte, e aí ele foi me empurrando um pouquinho mais para frente", relembrou.

Segundo a jovem, a corrente da bicicleta chegou a cair durante o ataque. Nesse momento, ela conseguiu olhar para o motociclista, que usava capacete.

"Só consegui ver o olhar dele e é um olhar assustador, inclusive, estou sem dormir desde o dia já que aconteceu, porque é a única coisa que vem na cabeça", lamentou.

A jovem explicou que a rua é deserta e, por isso, ficou extremamente assustada pensando em tudo que poderia acontecer. "Fui embora chorando o caminho inteiro até a minha casa".

Para as vítimas, a sensação é de insegurança . "É um sentimento de tristeza, de raiva, de angústia. A ansiedade vai lá em cima, nunca passei por isso. Sempre andei sozinha, de bicicleta, a pé, nunca aconteceu isso", afirmou Jéssica.

articles.title: Dois homens são presos com 700 kg de abacates furtados de fazenda | G1
articles.standfirst: Dupla foi localizada pela GCM durante patrulhamento em Vargem Grande do Sul; veículo estava carregado com 35 caixas da fruta. Caso foi registrado na madrugada de terça-feira (29).
articles.summary: Dupla foi localizada pela GCM durante patrulhamento em Vargem Grande do Sul; veículo estava carregado com 35 caixas da fruta. Caso foi registrado na madrugada de terça-feira (29).
articles.body:
Dois homens, de 42 e 45 anos, foram presos em flagrante na madrugada desta terça-feira (29) suspeitos de furtar cerca de 700 quilos de abacates de uma fazenda em São Sebastião da Grama (SP).

Segundo a Guarda Civil Municipal (GCM) de Vargem Grande do Sul , uma denúncia levou os agentes até os suspeitos, que são de Aguaí (SP).

Durante o patrulhamento, os guardas localizaram o carro em Vargem Grande do Sul, pouco antes das 2h. O veículo estava carregado com aproximadamente 36 caixas de abacates, totalizando cerca de 700 quilos da fruta.

Dupla é detida com 700 kg de abacates furtados de fazenda de São Sebastião da Grama — Foto: GCM / Vargem Grande do Sul

Ainda de acordo com a GCM, os dois homens já teriam furtado frutas da mesma fazenda em outras ocasiões.

Os suspeitos foram detidos e levados para as providências policiais. O veículo foi apreendido e os abacates foram devolvidos ao proprietário da fazenda.

articles.title: Estupro coletivo na Universidade de Cornell: investigação é reaberta | G1
articles.standfirst: Detalhes recém-publicados sobre o suposto incidente alimentaram acusações de que a universidade foi muito indulgente e reacendeu debate sobre as agressões sexuais em campi universitários.
articles.summary: Detalhes recém-publicados sobre o suposto incidente alimentaram acusações de que a universidade foi muito indulgente e reacendeu debate sobre as agressões sexuais em universidades.
articles.body:
A casa da fraternidade Chi Phi na Universidade Cornell em Ithaca, Nova York — Foto: AP/Heather Ainsworth

Promotores de Justiça dos Estados Unidos reabriram, nesta segunda-feira (28), uma investigação sobre um suposto estupro coletivo na prestigiada Universidade de Cornell, após denúncias de que a instituição não puniu adequadamente os acusados.

A suposta vítima afirmou em uma ação civil apresentada este mês que em 2024 foi drogada com cetamina, agredida e estuprada por sete membros da fraternidade Chi Phi, um clube social para estudantes homens da universidade.

Cornell fechou a fraternidade e suspendeu temporariamente os estudantes envolvidos, vários dos quais foram expulsos posteriormente.

Os detalhes recém-publicados sobre o suposto incidente alimentaram acusações de que a universidade foi muito indulgente e reacendeu o debate sobre as agressões sexuais em campi universitários.

Matthew Van Houten, promotor do distrito do condado de Tompkins, em Nova York, disse que planeja apresentar acusações criminais contra os sete homens acusados.

Ele acrescentou que seu escritório decidiu, em 2024, não processar o caso porque o depoimento da vítima não estabelecia a falta de consentimento, mas que agora resolveu fazê-lo à luz de suas novas alegações.

"Reconheço a realidade de que vítimas de agressões sexuais podem precisar de anos de terapia e recuperação para processar plenamente e compreender o que lhes aconteceu", disse Van Houten em comunicado.

Kyle Kimball, vice-presidente de relações universitárias de Cornell, afirmou que a universidade, integrante da prestigiosa Ivy League, apoia a decisão de reabrir a investigação, mas rejeitou a alegação, formulada na ação civil, de que teria sido oferecida aos suspeitos a oportunidade de escrever redações para reparar sua conduta.

A ação civil de 101 páginas apresentada em Nova York traz detalhes sobre a suposta agressão à mulher, cuja identidade permanece protegida. A queixa indica que a vítima sofreu "graves transtornos emocionais e psicológicos" e busca uma indenização financeira da instituição e dos sete suspeitos.

O caso gerou grande comoção pública, sendo condenado por figuras como a atriz britânica Florence Pugh e a deputada democrata Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez.

articles.title: America's Best New Restaurant Is In Tempe, According To Yelp Users
articles.summary: This year, an Arizona city with a population of less than 200,000 has come on top on a ranked restaurant list.
articles.body:
The best food city in America is constantly up for debate, though the contenders tend to be the country's biggest cities: New York, Chicago, Los Angeles, San Francisco… This year, an Arizona city with a population of less than 200,000 has come on top on a ranked restaurant list.

Yelp's annual rankings of the best new restaurants in America is out, and the top spot goes to Filthy Animal in Tempe. Named for a reference from the 1990 film Home Alone, Chef Rene Vargas's new restaurant centers around open-fire cooking to create globally influenced dishes.

Diners rave about starters like Vargas' " pillowy soft " milk bread with miso tomato butter, tuna pineapple ceviche with plantain chips, and beef tartarevwith grill-smoked ingredients. For entrees, Yelpers recommend a " genius " lemongrass half chicken with jalapeño jam and eternal dream-worthy lobster mac and cheese with thick noodles. Roasted oysters topped with gochujang butter and Chihuahua queso have also been dubbed " divine ."

"What's exciting about this year's list is that it validates what we've been seeing in Yelp data all year. Indian cuisine is gaining broader recognition and enthusiasm across the U.S., just as we predicted," say Tara Lewis, Yelp's Trend Expert. "Restaurants like Ambassadors Clubhouse and Eylan showcase how diners are embracing bold, globally rooted flavors in new ways. From culturally reimagined steakhouses to brunch evolving into a true destination experience, this year's class reflects a dining scene that's more adventurous, more personal, and more community-driven than ever."

Second on the list, a high-profile spot in a bigger city: Firstborn in Los Angeles. Already rated by the Michelin Guide, Firstborn is owned by Chef Anthony Wang, a first-generation American who serves a $68 contemporary Chinese prix-fixe menu, with optional add-ons.

Next on the list is Los Angeles' direct competitor: New York. Limusina, the extravagant and fun Mexican-inspired restaurant by Quality Branded ranks third for Yelp users favorite new restaurants. Built in a former parking garage, Limusina is known for its fun, shareable dishes like queso fundido flambee lit on fire tableside, long-bone short rib quesabirria drizzled with cheese at the table, and a piñata salad that requires plenty of fun fork action.

California restaurants cinched the fourth and fifth places in Yelp's rankings. Eylan in Menlo Park in California's Bay Area is run by 2026 James Beard award finalists Chef Srijith Gopinathan and restaurateur Ayesha Thapar. The restaurant offers an Indian tasting menu with vegan and vegetarian options, and holds a Michelin Bib Gourmand.

The fine dining restaurant Lilo in Carlsbad, California, earned a Michelin star just two months after opening, and is next on the list. Sixth place goes to 1587 Prime in Kansas City, Missouri, a steakhouse known for its celebrity co-ownership (NFL players Patrick Mahomes and Travis Kelce). Seventh is Bar Boheme, Las Vegas in Las Vegas, followed by Mezcla in Columbus, Ohio. Number nine is Dorothy's Downtown in Jacksonville, Florida and the tenth best restaurant is the high-end Indian restaurant Ambassadors Clubhouse in New York City, an extension of the original London restaurant.

articles.title: Pakistan’s Hangor-class submarine fires missile, raising stakes in the Arabian Sea
articles.summary: Even as India's long-delayed P-75(I) project for six new-generation submarines continues to hang fire, Pakistan on Sunday announced that its newly
articles.body: Even as India's long-delayed P-75(I) project for six new-generation submarines continues to hang fire, Pakistan on Sunday announced that its newly inducted Chinese-built AIP submarine had successfully test-fired an anti-ship cruise missile in the North Arabian Sea. Sources in the Indian defence establishment identified the missile as the Chinese YJ-18, assessed to be derived from the Russian Klub family, with some variants claiming a strike range of up to 540 km.The test comes just 12 days after a Pakistani naval vessel and an Indian warship collided in the North Arabian Sea on September 15. India had lodged a strong protest, holding that PNS Hunain approached the Indian warship at high speed and manoeuvred unsafely. Islamabad disputed the account. The Indian warship continued its mission, while PNS Hunain was forced to return to port.Hangor, the first of eight submarines Pakistan is acquiring from China, was commissioned at Sanya at the end of April and arrived in Karachi in June. Four of the eight are being built in China and four in Karachi. Crucially, the submarine is fitted with Air Independent Propulsion, which allows it to remain submerged for two to three weeks at a stretch instead of surfacing every few days to recharge batteries, making it significantly harder to detect and hunt.Submarines armed with cruise missiles add long-range strike capability to one of the hardest platforms to detect in naval warfare. Unlike torpedoes, cruise missiles let a submarine engage targets well beyond the immediate maritime battlespace, including, in some configurations, targets deep inland. The combination of stealth, mobility and long-range missiles allows submarines to approach contested waters covertly and strike without exposing their position, a template the US Navy has long used with Tomahawk-armed Virginia-class submarines.India's own undersea fleet, by comparison, is under strain. The Navy currently operates 16 conventional diesel-electric submarines across the Kalvari, Sindhughosh and Shishumar classes. Four Sindhughosh-class boats have already been retired, while the Shishumar class has gone through a mid-life upgrade meant to extend service by roughly a decade. Only the six Kalvari-class submarines, based on the French Scorpène design, are expected to receive a DRDO-developed indigenous AIP system in the coming years. The Navy's original plan to field 24 conventional submarines by 2030 has slipped considerably, partly due to delays in the P-75(I) programme, a roughly Rs 70,000 crore tender for six to nine Type-214 submarines with AIP, though Mazagon Dock and Germany's TKMS have now cleared technical evaluation.On the nuclear side, India operates three Arihant-class submarines with a fourth undergoing trials, carrying K-4 and K-5 missiles as the sea-based leg of India's nuclear triad. Work is underway on the larger S5-class submarines, expected to carry K-6 missiles with ranges beyond 5,000 km. The Navy is also pursuing Project-76, featuring a modified indigenous AIP system, alongside Project-77 for indigenous nuclear attack submarines and a separate lease of a Russian nuclear attack submarine, though all remain years from fruition. Despite Pakistan's latest test, the Indian Navy continues to hold overwhelming numerical superiority over its neighbour in this domain.

articles.title: The AI revolution will go wherever there's electricity — and China knows it
articles.summary: President Donald Trump's solar and battery storage push aims to secure energy dominance and fuel the AI data centers America needs to outpace China.
articles.body: Despite the recent surge in AI doomerism, President Donald Trump is right to maintain his strong support for data centers. As he notes: "China couldn’t be happier" if we were to turn our backs on these centers as a nation, which would effectively let the Chinese Communist Party win the AI race. As Energy Secretary Chris Wright said in July, "The country that leads in artificial intelligence in the coming years and decades ahead will be the global superpower." Victory means capturing trillions of dollars in national wealth, securing an advantage in military technology and gaining enormous leverage in international affairs. An energy bottleneck could pose a serious risk to America’s AI lead. We need data centers to train and run top-tier AI models, and those centers need a lot of electricity. In 2024, they accounted for over 4% of electricity use, and their consumption is expected to more than double by 2030. CHINA IS BUILDING AN AI WAR MACHINE. WASHINGTON MUST WAKE UP BEFORE IT’S TOO LATE Ensuring there is sufficient supply and generation to meet the soaring demand is imperative to staying in the lead. Solar should be a key part of that equation. New data centers need energy right now. New gas turbines and other large power projects can take years to bring online. Solar and battery projects can generally be deployed much faster, making them especially useful for meeting the near-term surge in electricity demand. Solar power has been closely associated with the environmental left, because for decades, Democrats largely sold solar as a climate policy, often with no concern for cost, for whether the panels themselves were made in America or whether deployment strengthened a supply chain dominated by China. However, the strategic equation has changed. Under the Trump Administration, the case for solar isn’t about "going green." It’s about reindustrialization, energy security, technological leadership and the national interest. The Trump Administration recognizes the value that producing more domestic batteries brings to our energy security. That’s why the Energy Department recently backed 220 megawatts of new battery storage in Puerto Rico, which is enough to provide backup electricity for more than 100,000 customers during power shortages. This project will use American-made battery technology — strengthening the grid and our domestic energy supply chain at the same time. Thanks in large part to the work of the Trump administration, a very different picture of solar has emerged from the one encountered a decade ago. By creating the conditions for investment in Made in America panels and components, Washington is turning what was once a China-dependent industry into another source of American energy security and industrial strength. In fact, private industry has poured $18.2 billion into building a domestic solar supply chain since 2022, and cell production was recently reshored for the first time in five years. Battery storage in the U.S. just topped 52 gigawatts of capacity, and it's been growing about 70% a year for three years straight. Thanks to these batteries, the American people now have significant access to this power not just when the sun is out at midday, but also in the evenings when America’s workers return home and turn on their lights and air conditioning. President Trump’s agenda has created an opportunity to support the domestic U.S. solar industry that we should take advantage of. By emphasizing solar as part of a broader all of the above energy dominance strategy, we can reinvigorate the domestic supply chains and spur U.S. production necessary to support our national interests, in both energy and AI policy. CHINA ‘THROWING GASOLINE ON THE FIRE’ IN AI DATA CENTERS RACE, SAY LAWMAKERS Building up secure domestic supply chains for solar has the added advantage of insulating the U.S. against future energy shocks because the fuel these panels run on doesn’t require pipelines or tankers. Iran might be able to mine the Strait of Hormuz, but it can’t block out the sun. Call it an Arsenal of Democracy for the AI age. At a moment when the country needs vastly more electricity, American companies are answering with real capital and real factories, and Washington is finally clearing a path for them to build here at home. articles.title: Malaysia begins sending back Rohingya refugees despite safety warnings
articles.summary: About 1,500 refugees are to be sent back in the first phase, despite criticism from rights groups.
articles.body:
Malaysia has begun sending nearly 1,500 Rohingya refugees back to Myanmar, describing their return as voluntary despite warnings from the United Nations and rights groups that Myanmar remains unsafe for them.

Dozens of buses arrived under police escort at a stadium near the Lumut naval base in northwestern Malaysia on Tuesday, the AFP news agency reported. Journalists were barred from the grounds. The passengers were expected to be processed before being taken to the base and transported to Myanmar by ship.

The Myanmar army has repeatedly cracked down on the country’s Rohingya minority, including a wave of violence in 2017 that many rights groups have described as genocide, and which set off a major refugee crisis, with hundreds of thousands of Rohingya fleeing to Bangladesh, Malaysia, India and other neighbouring nations. Myanmar does not officially recognise the Rohingya as an ethnic community with local roots, instead describing them as “Bengalis” — in effect, calling them Bangladeshi migrants.

As of February 2026, Malaysia had more than 126,144 Rohingya refugees. Bangladesh hosts the most Rohingya refugees — more than 1.2 million.

Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim said in July that Myanmar had agreed to take back 5,000 Rohingya, leaving a question about who is being sent back. The nearly 1,500 picked for repatriation on Tuesday are part of the group. The Ministry of Home Affairs said two Myanmar naval warships and a hospital ship would be used.

The UN High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) said it had no role in the operation and warned that continuing conflict and violence in Myanmar meant conditions for safe and dignified returns did not exist. “Any refugee return must be voluntary, based on an informed decision, and take place in conditions of safety and dignity,” it told the Reuters news agency.

Malaysia’s Home Ministry declined to comment on the warning, referring to its earlier statement that the returns were voluntary.

Rights advocates question whether people held in detention can freely choose to return to a country they fled.

“The genocide has never stopped. Sending Rohingya back to this is not repatriation,” Nay San Lwin, cochair of the Arakan Rohingya National Council (ARNC), a group representing the Rohingya, told Al Jazeera. “It is sending people back to a killing field. We call on Malaysia to halt all returns of Rohingya to Myanmar until it is safe.”

He argued that Malaysia’s decision to send refugees back to Myanmar came at a time when intense fighting was taking place between the army and rebel groups, including the Arakan Army.

“The Myanmar military has lost control of much of the Rohingya homeland, and its fighting with the Arakan Army is still ongoing, with Rohingya caught in the middle. Both the military and the Arakan Army are committing atrocities against the Rohingya,” he said.

Ro Mayyu Islam, founding Chair of the Center for Rohingya Crisis Studies based in Cox’s Bazaar, Bangladesh, also opposed the repatriation under the present conditions.

“Do not confuse repatriation with resolution. Moving Rohingya from Malaysian detention centres to Myanmar does not solve the Rohingya crisis. Address the conditions that forced us to flee, and then make the return genuinely safe, voluntary and sustainable,” he told Al Jazeera from Cox’s Bazaar.

“We are not asking the world to keep us refugees. We are demanding the right to return home as equal human beings with citizenship, security, dignity and fundamental rights.”

Meanwhile, Doctors Without Borders (MSF) has urged Malaysia to halt the returns and disclose who was being sent back and what risks each person faced. “Refugees should not be returned to places they’ve fled and where their lives are at risk,” the organisation said.

More than 160 civil society organisations also called for the repatriation to stop, citing violence and the risk that Rohingya could be pressed into armed groups. Their warning comes as Myanmar’s military fights the Arakan Army in Rakhine state, the region from which many Rohingya fled.

Myanmar’s government has promised “safe and dignified” returns for the Rohingya. Meanwhile, Malaysian Communications Minister Fahmi Fadzil has said the country would not return people if they faced persecution or threats to their lives.

For Rohingya who have already gone back, the question is what awaits them after arrival. Ismail, 25, told AFP he left his work at a fish market in Malaysia amid arrests and rising hostility towards Rohingya. Now jobless in Yangon, he relies on relatives and still lacks full citizenship. “We are the most discriminated people,” he said. In Rakhine, a Rohingya activist identified as Mohammad feared returnees could be sent to displacement camps in a region still affected by fighting and disease.

The returns follow growing pressure on Rohingya in Malaysia. In July, authorities detained more than 100 people who gathered outside UNHCR’s office in Kuala Lumpur after facing eviction from an informal settlement in Penang. They were later released when officials confirmed they held UN documents, AFP reported. Malaysia is not a party to the 1951 Refugee Convention and does not formally recognise refugee status.

Anwar has said he intends to invite Myanmar’s Senior General Min Aung Hlaing, who led the military during the 2017 crackdown, to Malaysia to help accelerate the returns.

articles.title: Met Police officer charged after BBC Panorama Charing Cross investigation
articles.summary: The police watchdog began an investigation into alleged misconduct at Charing Cross police station in London as a result of a BBC Panorama investigation.
articles.body:
A Metropolitan Police officer has become the first person to be charged as a result of a BBC Panorama investigation into alleged misconduct at Charing Cross police station in London.

Sgt Sadiq Al-Hasani, 37, has been charged with perverting the course of justice.

He will appear at Westminster Magistrates' Court on Wednesday.

In a statement, the Met Police said the charge related to an allegation Sgt Al-Hasani, who was attached to Central West Command Unit, "deliberately sought to discourage another officer from making a statement to the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC)".

The IOPC had begun an investigation following the broadcast on 1 October 2025 of BBC Panorama – Undercover in the Police.

As part of the programme, a BBC journalist went undercover working in the custody suite, secretly filming a number of officers making racist comments and bragging about violence used against suspects.

Al-Hasani was charged on 13 August in relation to an incident on 2 October 2025.

In a statement, the IOPC said Sgt Al-Hasani allegedly approached a junior officer, who was a potential key witness in the wider Charing Cross investigation, with the intention to obstruct or interfere with the probe.

He remains suspended from duty, the Met said.

The IOPC began its investigation after a mandatory conduct referral from the Met on 3 October.

As part of this, the IOPC reviewed footage gathered as part of the programme which was not broadcast.

Its investigation finished in June, at which point it decided to refer a file of evidence to the Crown Prosecution Service.

According to the IOPC, 15 officers have been found to have committed gross misconduct. All except one of the 15, a former PC, have been barred from policing.

Investigations continue into the conduct of a further 14 officers or police staff.

articles.title: In 2019, a Miami artist built a ceramic underwater reef to give coral a place to grip; her sculptures became a nursery-like habitat for reef animals instead of only gallery art
articles.summary: Discover Beatriz Chachamovits' innovative ceramic underwater reef, designed to mimic coral and provide a habitat for marine life, while addressing critical issues like coral bleaching and plastic pollution. Join the movement to preserve our oceans.
articles.body: Beatriz Chachamovits is a Brazilian-born artist based in Miami who created To Replenish With Water as an artificial reef for the Underwater Museum of Art off Florida's Gulf Coast. The work depicts bleached corals and sponges that are mixed with forms resembling plastic waste, with the expectation that living coral would eventually grow over its surface.The sculpture was part of the museum's 2019 installation, which placed 12 new artworks underwater near Grayton Beach State Park in South Walton, Florida. The Underwater Museum of Art was created in partnership with the South Walton Artificial Reef Association, and the sculptures were intended to serve a purpose beyond attracting divers. The organisations describe the museum as a way to create marine habitat while also providing cultural and educational opportunities.Chachamovits' piece was made to resemble several Florida coral species, including elkhorn, staghorn, brain and fire corals, as well as tube, vase and barrel sponges. The sculpture was primarily modelled from clay by making use of a 3D printer and then cast in clean white cement. The white surface was intentional, and represented coral bleaching at the starting point of the installation rather than trying to imitate a healthy, colourful reef.The artwork was meant to change underwaterThe Underwater Museum of Art says that the forms were designed to be covered over time by new and healthy corals, and the artificial object would gradually lose its original white appearance as organisms colonised the structure. That approach fits Chachamovits' wider work since her practice combines ceramics with marine research and education, and she has repeatedly used sculptures to represent coral bleaching, plastic pollution and changes to reef ecosystems. Her own account of the project says that she became interested in artificial reefs after creating To Replenish With Water and has since focused on the structures as a way to provide surfaces where corals can attach and grow. Chachamovits describes artificial reefs as potential spaces where corals can attach, while reef animals can use the structures as habitat. The sculpture’s intended role was to provide a hard underwater structure that could be colonised over time.The Underwater Museum of Art sits in the Gulf of Mexico roughly a mile from shore, at a depth of about 58 feet, and divers need certification to visit the submerged works. The 2019 deployment added the work to a collection that already treated underwater sculpture as more than an art installation, and the museum's partnership with the artificial reef organisation meant that the pieces were selected and placed with marine habitat in mind. Chachamovits' sculpture was one of several works in that year's group, alongside structures such as Depth of Decision, which is a series of concrete doorways designed with openings that could be used by marine life.Her ceramics became part of a larger reef projectChachamovits continued developing work around the same idea after the 2019 installation, and her projects have included ceramic representations of endangered Florida reef species surrounded by objects such as bottles, cigarette butts, plastic caps and discarded toothbrushes. In those works, the waste is also made from ceramic rather than being actual marine debris.Through her Modeling the Reef project, she has used sculpting activities to teach children about coral ecosystems. Her larger body of work examines the physical changes taking place on reefs through objects that can be seen and handled rather than through scientific charts alone. For To Replenish With Water, however, the most unusual part of the work remains its intended transformation, as the sculpture was placed underwater as a representation of a bleached reef, with the expectation that living organisms would eventually cover the manufactured surface and turn it into part of the surrounding marine habitat.You use AI every day. articles.summary: NEW DELHI: The Israel Defense Forces (IDF) on Sunday released aerial footage that it said showed a Hamas fighter using young child to transfer weapons
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The Israel Defense Forces (IDF) on Sunday released aerial footage that it said showed a Hamas fighter using young child to transfer weapons into a civilian home in central Gaza.The footage, recorded by an Israeli drone and shared by the IDF, appears to show a young boy struggling to carry a large rifle while a suspected militant directs him down a street.At one point, the child appears to stagger under the weight of the weapon. However, the video could not be independently verified.The IDF said the incident took place during operations in central Gaza and alleged that the child was being used as a human shield to prevent Israeli forces from striking the suspected militant and the weapons being transferred.“The terrorist exploited the child, using him as a human shield to transfer the weapons, in an attempt to prevent the IDF from striking and thwarting their transfer,” the IDF said in a statement on Sunday.“Upon identifying the presence of a child, the IDF refrained from carrying out any strikes against the terrorist,” it added.The Israeli military described the incident as another example of the “systematic exploitation of children by terrorist organizations for terrorist purposes, in violation of international law.”The IDF has repeatedly accused Hamas of operating from densely populated civilian areas in Gaza and of placing weapons, command centres and rocket launchers near schools and residential neighbourhoods.Hamas has denied such allegations, arguing that Gaza is one of the most densely populated places in the world and that military activity therefore naturally takes place near civilian areas, the Jerusalem Post reported.Hamas leaders have also said that Israel, as the occupying power of the Gaza Strip, bears the legal responsibility for protecting civilians and children.You use AI every day. articles.title: Mass migration eroding Western sovereignty, immigration expert warns
articles.summary: President Donald Trump challenged the United Nations General Assembly on mass migration, but an expert says the sovereignty crisis runs deeper.
articles.body: Unchecked mass migration, particularly in Western nations where millions have settled after leaving third-world countries, tends to erode national sovereignty, one expert said — an issue President Donald Trump highlighted during his speech last week in front of other world leaders at the United Nations General Assembly. As migrants continue to reach Western shores, those countries are grappling with stretched resources and tensions between newly arrived immigrants, some here illegally, and the native population, many of whom feel their best interests and cultural identity are being overlooked by government bureaucrats. The pushback stands in contrast to the vision of "global citizenship" advocated by entities like the World Economic Forum and U.N. initiatives, set against the rise of nationalist opposition led by figures like Trump. Much of the push for illegal migration comes from non-governmental groups and other grant-making networks, Lora Ries, director of the Border Security and Immigration Center at The Heritage Foundation, told Fox News Digital. LIZ PEEK: CAN TRUMP MAKE THE UN GREAT AGAIN DESPITE ITS GLOBALIST AGENDA? "It's no coincidence that we've seen the same tactics in a handful of countries at the same time, whether that's to the U.K., to France, to Germany, other parts of Western Europe, or to the U.S., particularly during Biden's four years," said Ries. "And what that does is it erodes the sovereignty of the nation-state. So no longer do people in a nation get to decide who's coming, how many, for what reason, and for how long, and whether people are complying with our laws." Groups like the U.N., World Economic Forum and International Organization for Migration (IOM) all advocate for managed, regular and lawful migration while treating mobility as a natural economic and demographic reality. However, European countries are being stretched thin as migrants continue to change the demographic and cultural landscape within their borders, critics of mass migration say. Ries cited the lack of assimilation among some migrants, the formation of ethnic enclaves, language shifts, and hesitation by law enforcement and elected officials to address the matter driven by political correctness. TENS OF THOUSANDS FLOOD STREETS TO PROTEST SPAIN BORDER CRISIS "And now we've got Western countries like the U.K. and France really teetering on, are they still the same countries?" said Ries. "The U.S. is on the same path — we're just further behind. And so now … we have to ask ourselves, ‘Do we want to continue down the same path that the U.K. has been on? Or do we want to get off this path?’" During Trump's speech last week at the United Nations General Assembly, he reiterated his administration's hardline position on defending American borders while criticizing the U.N. TRUMP TO ZERO-IN ON IRAN NUCLEAR THREAT, GAZA PLAN AND UN OVERHAUL IN WORLD STAGE SPEECH "It is deeply ironic that the United Nations has an entire institution, the UNESCO group of people and countries, devoted to protecting cultural heritage — yet, with their ceaseless promotion of mass migration, these globalists are actively destroying the greatest cultures and most extraordinary heritage in history," he said. "There is no human right to illegal immigration, but there is a right to remain a sovereign nation." The IOM, an arm of the U.N., states that it's committed to the principle that humane and orderly migration benefits migrants and society. Ries cited the U.N. 2030 agenda, the universal action plan adopted in 2015 by its member states to combat poverty and fight climate change. At the heart of the plan are 17 sustainable development goals. "They view mass migration as a way to achieve some … all of those 17 goals of sustainable development. But it's certainly not sustainable for the nation-states that are being overrun," Ries said. DHS' TOP LAWYER THREATENS PENALTIES FOR ATTORNEYS CLOGGING ASYLUM SYSTEM One aspect of the mass migration crisis is the asylum process, which critics say is ripe for abuse, allowing people into countries despite not having a valid claim and rendering asylum and refugee protection meaningless. "We need to get back to the original objective grounds for persecution, which is it has to be a government actor persecuting you on account of your race, your religion, your nationality or political opinion," Ries said. "And really get the meaning of persecution back into a box, because right now it is so watered down." articles.title: Trump ‘surprised’ after Britain releases men detained near base used by U.S. forces
articles.summary: President Donald Trump said he was surprised after British police released on bail five men arrested in connection with a huge security operation near an air base used by the U.S.
articles.body: President Donald Trump said he was surprised after British police released on bail five men arrested in connection with a huge security operation near an air base used by the U.S. Air Force to facilitate strikes on Iran. Later, Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the incident “clearly involves the hands of a foreign actor” — an allegation British officials have not confirmed. “I would have said, ‘Don’t let them have bail,’” Trump said in the Oval Office on Monday. “I’m surprised that they released them, I wouldn’t have done that.” Trump also indicated U.S. officials were cooperating with their British counterparts on the case. “Look, they’ve been very good. They are working with us very closely,” he said, adding that the United States knew “everything” about the suspects. The five men, all British nationals in their 20s from London, were arrested Sunday on suspicion of terrorism and explosives offenses after three vehicles were seen moving toward RAF Fairford, a British air force station about 90 minutes west of London. Counterterrorism police took over the case after a major incident was declared, disrupting life in the normally quiet, rural community of the Cotswolds. On Monday, British counterterrorism officials said the men had been released on bail after “extensive interviews and inquiries.” The investigation was not over, counterterrorism police head Laurence Taylor said, and “multiple lines of inquiry” were still being probed. No charges have been filed against the men. Taylor said the three vans that the suspects were traveling in have been “subject to extensive examination with the support of military assets and forensic experts.” He did not say if any explosives have been found, as the question remains about what was inside the vans. According to several British reports, no explosives were found. NBC News reached out to counterterrorism police for clarification Tuesday but did not receive a response. On Sunday, counterterrorism police said the men had been arrested on suspicion of committing offenses under the Explosives Act, a British legislation dating back to 1875 that regulates manufacturing, keeping, selling, carrying and importing of gunpowder and explosive substances. The men were further arrested on suspicion of preparation of a terrorist act. The incident prompted questions about whether a foreign actor could be involved — in particular, Iran, after the country’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps warned Britain this summer that RAF Fairford could be a “legitimate target.” It came months after then-Prime Minister Keir Starmer gave permission for the U.S. to use its bases for “specific and limited defensive” operations against Iran. The Iranian Embassy in Britain denied any involvement Monday. During an appearance on Fox News later Monday, Rubio said that “what happened, what almost happened, what could have happened in the U.K. over the weekend, is a very serious situation.” “There’s a lot more news that’ll come out on this in the days to come,” he added. Taylor, with the United Kingdom’s counterterrorism police, noted there had been “significant interest in whether the current geopolitical context has a bearing on this incident.” The investigators are keeping an open mind, he said. “Be assured we are considering this from every possible angle, including that this may be actively committed by proxies or individuals either knowingly or unknowingly working on behalf of a foreign state,” he added.

articles.title: Someone has been secretly poisoning Lake Tahoe trees since 2022 as 28 are already targeted; now community offers $147,000 to catch culprit
articles.summary: Someone has been repeatedly targeting mature pine trees at Burnt Cedar Beach in Incline Village, Nevada, on the north shore of Lake Tahoe, with
articles.body: Someone has been repeatedly targeting mature pine trees at Burnt Cedar Beach in Incline Village, Nevada, on the north shore of Lake Tahoe, with investigators documenting 28 affected trees since 2022. Six trees were damaged in 2022, another six in 2024 and 16 more were targeted in 2026. At least 10 of the trees have died, according to the Los Angeles Times, while the total estimated loss is more than $300,000. With no suspect publicly identified, the Incline Village General Improvement District and private donors have offered a combined $147,000 reward for information leading to an arrest and successful prosecution. The repeated attacks have turned the case into a years-long mystery for the Lake Tahoe community.28 Lake Tahoe trees targeted by poisoning since 2022The Washoe County Sheriff's Office says 28 trees have been affected across three separate periods, with investigators treating the incidents as connected. Six trees were damaged in 2022, six more in 2024 and another 16 were discovered in 2026.The latest incidents occurred on May 26, July 23 and August 2. Four affected trees were discovered in May, two more in July and another 10 in August. The trees are located around Burnt Cedar Beach, a residents-only recreation area in Incline Village.The repeated targeting of trees over several years has prompted officials to increase surveillance and investigate whether the same person or group is responsible for the incidents.How the trees were poisonedInvestigators found evidence that several of the trees had been deliberately damaged. Holes were drilled near the roots of some trees, while substances were found around the affected areas. Soil samples were collected and sent for testing as investigators attempted to determine exactly what was used.The Washoe County Sheriff's Office has said the substance responsible for the poisoning had not been identified. IVGID previously said a substance found during the May investigation was believed to be diesel fuel, but authorities have not publicly confirmed diesel as the substance used in all 28 cases.Local reporting has also cited 72 drilled holes across the affected trees, although that figure came from a representative of Friends of Burnt Cedar Beach rather than directly from investigators.At least 10 trees have diedThe attacks have already resulted in significant damage. The Los Angeles Times reported that at least 10 of the 28 targeted trees had died. Some of the affected trees were mature specimens that had stood at the beach for decades.IVGID estimates the value of the 28 targeted trees at more than $300,000. Arborists have been assessing the damaged trees and working to determine which ones can still be saved.The loss of mature trees can have a long-term effect on the landscape because replacement trees require decades to reach a similar size. Officials have therefore treated the incidents as both a criminal investigation and an environmental concern.Community offers $147,000 rewardThe community has now put up a $147,000 reward for information that leads to an arrest and successful prosecution.IVGID is contributing $25,000, while $122,000 has been pledged by private donors associated with Friends of Burnt Cedar Beach. The reward is intended to encourage anyone with information about the attacks to contact investigators.A separate $1,000 Secret Witness reward is also available for information leading to an arrest and prosecution.The main reward has a deadline of March 31, 2027. Information must ultimately lead to a successful prosecution within two years of being provided to qualify for the reward.Police are searching for the culpritThe Washoe County Sheriff's Office is investigating the case under number 26-4225. Authorities have not publicly identified a suspect or announced an arrest.Investigators are asking anyone who may have witnessed suspicious activity around Burnt Cedar Beach or who has information about the affected trees to come forward.The Sheriff's Office has said the estimated financial damage could support felony-level charges against whoever is responsible.Officials have also increased security around the affected area. Additional cameras have been installed to help detect further incidents and potentially identify anyone attempting to damage more trees.Why someone may be targeting the treesThe motive remains unknown. One theory reported by local and national media is that the trees could have been targeted because they obstruct views of Lake Tahoe or affect the value of nearby properties.Some of the affected trees have been described as being positioned along sightlines toward the lake. That has prompted speculation among residents that improving views could be connected to the attacks.However, investigators have not publicly established that view improvement, property values or any other specific motive was behind the poisoning. The reason someone repeatedly targeted the trees remains part of the mystery.Burnt Cedar Beach remains openDespite the damage, Burnt Cedar Beach remains open to the public permitted to use the residents-only facility. IVGID has said there is no immediate threat to beachgoers from the tree-poisoning incidents.The focus is now on protecting the remaining trees while investigators try to establish exactly how the poisonings were carried out and who was responsible.The affected trees are being monitored, and arborists are assessing whether some can recover from the damage.A mystery dating back to 2022The investigation stretches back four years, beginning with six affected trees in 2022. Another six were targeted in 2024, followed by 16 in 2026.That pattern has left investigators examining whether the incidents form part of a deliberate campaign against trees at the same Lake Tahoe beach.With 28 trees affected, more than $300,000 in estimated damage and at least 10 trees reported dead, local officials and residents are now hoping the $147,000 reward will produce information that can break the case.For now, the person behind the attacks remains unidentified, while investigators continue examining evidence from the trees and the surrounding area.You use AI every day. articles.title: In 2004, a New York truck driver began cutting tiny buildings from balsa wood; 22 years later, his handmade New York of more than 300 sections entered a city museum
articles.summary: Discover the inspiring journey of Joe Macken, a truck driver who handcrafted an astonishing 800,000 miniature buildings representing New York City, now showcased at the Museum of the City of New York.
articles.body: For more than two decades, Joe Macken quietly built another New York in his spare time. A Queens-born truck driver with no formal training in architecture or model-making, Macken began constructing his handmade version of the city in 2004. According to the Museum of the City of New York, he started with the Comcast Building at 30 Rockefeller Plaza and then continued building neighbourhoods, landmarks and other parts of the city by hand using balsa wood, cardboard and glue. By 2025, the project had grown into a vast model covering about 50 by 27 feet and comprising more than 340 individual sections. In 2026, what began as a private project moved into the Museum of the City of New York as the exhibition He Built This City: Joe Macken’s Model.From a childhood memory to a basement projectMacken's fascination with miniature New York began when he was a child. According to CBS News, during a school visit to the Queens Museum, he saw the Panorama of the City of New York, the enormous model created for the 1964–65 World's Fair. The experience stayed with him for years. After moving from Long Island to the Albany area, he eventually began making his own version of the city from memory. The project started modestly, with Macken first building a model of 30 Rockefeller Plaza, better known as 30 Rock. Once that was finished, he made another building, then another, and eventually spent about a decade building out Midtown Manhattan.The materials were purposely simple. The main construction materials were balsa wood and cardboard; foam board and glue were used to create the landscape. There was no architectural studio behind the construction, and there were no professional model makers involved in the process. As he repeated the process, Macken became faster and more experienced. Buildings that once took him hours became more familiar to him. As the model grew from a few buildings to a full cityscape, it came to represent all five boroughs, as well as parts of New Jersey and Long Island.A city built from memoryThe model is not just a miniature New York; it also captures the city as Macken remembers it. That becomes clear from the buildings and landmarks he chose to include. Along with familiar sights such as the Empire State Building, Brooklyn Bridge, Yankee Stadium and the Statue of Liberty, the model features places that have a personal connection to him. The Twin Towers appear alongside One World Trade Center and newer buildings in Lower Manhattan, while the old Kosciuszko Bridge remains part of the miniature city even though it was demolished in 2017. Macken has also recreated one of his favourite Queens landmarks, adding a personal touch to a model that otherwise represents an entire city.The museum describes the sculpture as a personal architectural portrait of New York, combining geographic accuracy with Macken’s own impressions and choices. Binoculars in the gallery let visitors move from a view of the whole city to the smallest details of individual neighbourhoods. The sculpture’s scale makes its size easier to appreciate. Its area is approximately 1,350 square feet, and it consists of more than 300 sections. In this way, even a small residential house becomes a part of a larger system of streets and blocks, while well-known skyscrapers turn into tiny landmarks of a huge handmade environment.From a basement to a museumFor years, Macken’s miniature New York was something he built simply because he wanted to. He worked as a truck driver and spent his spare time adding to the model, piece by piece. The finished creation covers about 50 by 27 feet and is made up of more than 340 sections. It began reaching a much larger audience when Macken’s daughter started posting videos of it on TikTok. Millions of people watched the videos, bringing the basement project to the attention of the Museum of the City of New York.The museum eventually invited Macken to put the model on display. He Built This City opened in February 2026 and is scheduled to run until October 12, 2026. This is the first time the complete model has been shown publicly in New York City, the place it has been built to represent. In the Dinan Miller Gallery, visitors can look across the miniature skyline from above and then move closer to spot individual buildings and familiar landmarks.Part of the appeal is being able to see New York from a viewpoint that is difficult to have in the real city. Instead of moving through one street or neighbourhood at a time, visitors can view the miniature city as a whole and then look more closely for places they recognise. The model is therefore more than a miniature map of New York; it gives visitors another way to look at the city.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.
