articles.title: Hebridean families separated by 2,000 miles help find tiny boat
articles.summary: The families from the Hebrides played a part in finding the boat after its crossing of the Atlantic.
articles.body:
A schoolboy in the Western Isles has found a tiny sail boat which has spent 15 months crossing 2,000 miles of the Atlantic.

The craft, which is fitted with a GPS tracker, was launched in June last year from Portland, Maine, in the US, as part of a science project.

Shortly afterwards, it came ashore in Newfoundland, Canada. It was put to sea again in June this year by a school attended by the daughter of Gemma MacKinnon, who is originally from the isles.

Gemma alerted her family back home that the boat was headed for the Hebrides and Calum Iain MacNeil along with his dad, Donald, found it on a beach near their home in Barra on 7 September.

The boat, called Pie on the Tide, was launched as part of a schools science and environment project called the Miniboat Programme .

Once it became obvious the craft was heading for Barra, Gemma, who left the isles four years ago, was asked by her daughter's school if she might know anyone who could look out for it.

"I was able to send the co-ordinates to my brother whose girlfriend [Calum Iain's sister] is there and her family retrieved the mini boat," she said.

Michelle MacLean, deputy head teacher at Castlebay Primary School where Calum Iain is a pupil, said the boat was in "pretty good" condition after its almost 100 day-long, 2,000-mile crossing.

She added: "Calum and his father are at the moment looking at doing some preparation work to mend the sail, and there are a couple of other parts of it to make and then we're hoping to relaunch it."

Michelle said it was hoped the boat's next stop would be Norway.

articles.title: Malaysia gave refuge to Rohingya; now it wants them to go
articles.summary: Malaysia welcomed persecuted Muslim minority but now plans to send them back to Myanmar amid rising hate against them.
articles.body:
Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia – The children sitting cross-legged on the floor are a mix of ages but are all enrolled in one class out of necessity. Coming from Rohingya families, they are not allowed to access formal education and must rely upon the generosity of donors to support informal learning centres, such as the one they attend in a quiet neighbourhood in Kuala Lumpur.

“Because of their help, we can teach our kids here,” explained Riyadh Al Haq, a Rohingya human rights activist whose NGO runs the centre.

On one recent morning, they were busy learning the Quran, but lessons also cover a standard range of academic subjects.

They and their families are also not eligible to access the healthcare system, and their parents are not allowed to work and must rely on informal employment, such as at car washes, in restaurant kitchens and at courier services.

Still, life for the estimated 125,000 Rohingya who now call Malaysia home is better than the lives they left behind in Myanmar.

“Because of their [Malaysian people’s] kindness, our people can stay in this country. They can live here. We are more safe than in Myanmar,” Riyadh told Al Jazeera.

However, on Tuesday, the Malaysian government began the repatriation of an initial group of nearly 1,500 Rohingya to Myanmar. The operation has drawn renewed attention to the plight of the Rohingya people, regarded as one of the world’s most persecuted minorities. The Muslim ethnic group is essentially stateless because they are not recognised as citizens by Myanmar.

The repatriation has been criticised by the United Nations and international rights groups given the longstanding persecution of the Rohingya in their home state of Rakhine in western Myanmar. In 2017, the Myanmar military launched a brutal crackdown, forcing more than 700,000 Rohingya to flee, mostly to neighbouring Bangladesh.

The military campaign, which involved widespread destruction of Rohingya properties and the killing of thousands of people, is widely condemned as tantamount to a genocide. A case of genocide brought by The Gambia is under way at the International Court of Justice at The Hague. The verdict is expected next month or in November.

The Malaysian government insisted that all those returning are volunteers and their safety and wellbeing are guaranteed.

Critics of Kuala Lumpur’s policy said an ongoing civil war in Myanmar makes such guarantees meaningless. Myanmar descended into civil war after the military conducted a coup in 2021 and removed the democratically elected government of Nobel Peace Prize laureate Aung San Suu Kyi.

Malaysia’s government, led by Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim, has pledged to return 5,000 Myanmar nationals in what many see as a reversal of the country’s longstanding policy of leniency towards the presence of the Rohingya.

Not being a signatory to the 1951 United Nations Refugee Convention, Malaysia doesn’t grant the Rohingya refugee status but has taken a tolerant attitude towards their arrival.

Malaysians have a religious and cultural affinity with the Rohingya, and there is widespread sympathy for their plight. Many have extended an unofficial welcome to many migrants often making the perilous ocean journey on overcrowded boats.

But that attitude has started to change in recent years due to economic pressures and viral social media misinformation campaigns. Coordinated online petitions calling for the expulsion of refugees and other marginalised groups have garnered hundreds of thousands of signatures.

Nur Sadek, executive director of Rohingya Rights Response, has been monitoring social media content that spreads hateful and hurtful messaging about the Rohingya.

One content creator who has thousands of followers has posted a series of clips in which he mocks Rohingya openly to their faces while complaining to the camera about how they allegedly smell. In another clip produced by self-styled vigilantes, three men are seen stopping and questioning a Rohingya passer-by in the street.

“A lot of the community members are very afraid to go outside and to be recognised as a Rohingya,” Sadek said. “They are very afraid of being harassed by the local people and by some of the content creators.”

That fear also extends to employment, however menial the jobs might be, with some Malaysian businesses reportedly turning Rohingya away.

“Most of the Rohingya people have relied upon informal work, and even that informal work is inaccessible right now with the increase in hate and misinformation. And it is affecting the livelihoods of every Rohingya,” Sadek told Al Jazeera.

As Malaysia looks ahead to national elections early next year, political parties might find the Rohingya issue is too big a vote-winning opportunity to pass up. And the Rohingya, as they so often have, could find themselves the losers.

articles.title: Housing protests spread across Spain after 87-year-old is evicted from home
articles.summary: Housing protesters camped out in Madrid’s most iconic square awoke from their third night in the open to await details from the Spanish government on what it’s doing to tackle the crisis.
articles.body: MADRID — Housing protesters camped out in Madrid’s most iconic square awoke from their third night in the open to await details from the Spanish government on what it’s doing to tackle a crisis that has brought tens of thousands of people onto the streets in recent days. The protests and the encampment in Puerto del Sol followed the eviction of María del Carmen Abascal, 87, who was carried out on a stretcher from the apartment where she had lived for seven decades. Rising costs and a housing shortage are pricing many Spaniards out of the housing market, despite strong economic growth in Europe’s fourth-largest economy. The protesters are demanding stronger protections for tenants, measures to combat fraud and a ban on evictions when alternative housing is unavailable. Since the camp was set up on Saturday, the number of tents in the central square has increased. Smaller protest encampments have sprung up in other cities, from Seville and Málaga in the south to Santiago de Compostela in the north and Palma de Mallorca in the tourist-friendly Balearic Islands, drawing international attention to a long-running issue. Asked about the situation on Monday, Pope Leo XIV said it underscored the need for political leaders to find solutions to the housing crisis affecting many communities. “Maybe we have to insist that political leaders, authorities find a solution to this, because it’s obviously increasing and oftentimes we only react in the moment of an emergency,” he said, after admitting that he was not familiar with the case. “But we have to try to see what the systemic cause of the problem is and how to help.” Spain’s left-wing coalition government, led by Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez, is expected to present its decree at a news conference at 4 p.m. ET. Spain has had a housing law in place since 2023 that regulates rents and protects tenants, as well as allowing rent caps in high-demand areas at the request of local governments. Abascal, who has been hospitalized since she was carried out of her apartment on Wednesday, will be able to return home following a preliminary agreement reached Monday night with the company that owns the building in the upscale Retiro neighborhood. The proposal limits her rent to 30% of her income, meaning she will not pay more than the 500 euros ($570) per month she paid previously, her lawyer, Beatriz Duro, told reporters Tuesday. Spanish media reported that Abascal’s father first rented the property in 1956 and she continued as the tenant after her parents died, during which time there was a rent cap. The building changed ownership in 2018, and Abascal was offered the opportunity to buy the apartment but could not afford it, according to the Madrid Tenants’ Union, which organized Saturday’s protest. Urbagestión, an investment fund that later bought the unit, raised her monthly rent from 500 euros ($570) to 2,650 euros. It subsequently lowered the rent to 1,650 euros, which Abascal still could not afford on her pension, the union said.

articles.title: Are Houthis using new modified cruise missiles in Yemen’s war?
articles.summary: Experts say use of modified Iranian defence system could alter the balance in the fight for the Red Sea.
articles.body:
Yemen’s internationally recognised, Saudi-backed government has alleged that the Tehran-backed Houthis have modified Iranian air defence weapons into loitering cruise missiles with the assistance of Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC).

The Yemeni government has warned that the capability of such missiles – which operate on a heat-tracking system, it alleged – in practice threatens civilian air traffic over Yemen and the crucial Red Sea.

Meanwhile, the Houthis have ramped up attacks on Saudi Arabia as they fight Yemeni government forces. On Thursday, Riyadh said it intercepted six ballistic missiles aimed at Taif in western Saudi Arabia and the Yanbu port area on the Red Sea.

The Houthis also said they attacked “a sensitive target” in the Saudi capital, Riyadh, and Saudi Aramco facilities in Yanbu. Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said the group used ballistic and cruise missiles as well as drones in the two operations.

The Houthis were in open conflict with Yemen’s government and a Saudi-led coalition of Arab states from 2014 until a United Nations-brokered ceasefire was declared in 2022, but fighting has reignited in recent weeks with the Houthis taking the Red Sea coast of Yemen along with the strategically important city of Mocha and Mayyun Island in the Bab al-Mandeb strait at the southern entrance to the Red Sea.

In July, the armed group declared a naval blockade against Saudi Arabia in the Red Sea, essentially opening yet another theatre in the US-Israel war on Iran.

Since the closure of the critical Strait of Hormuz during the war, the Red Sea has become a vital alternative export route for the region’s biggest oil player, Saudi Arabia. Its East-West Pipeline , which carries oil from its eastern oilfields to the western port of Yanbu is only just restarting operations after damage inflicted by a drone attack this month.

So what do the Houthis’ latest missile capabilities mean for the region?

Brigadier General Majed al-Nazili, spokesperson for the Yemeni government forces, said the Houthis are using Iranian air defence weapons that pose a danger to all aircraft.

Al-Nazili said the weapons have been modified with the assistance of IRGC experts and are being used to strike aircraft and cruise missiles.

“These missiles move around for a period of up to 25 minutes per missile and operate using a thermal-tracking system and attack any heat source without the ability to distinguish between military or civilian targets,” he said in a statement.

“This constitutes a direct and serious threat to the safety of civil aviation and the lives of passengers,” al-Nazili added.

Why does Yemen’s government think regional airspace is under threat?

Al-Nazili noted that aircraft belonging to the United Nations or humanitarian organisations travelling via air routes over Yemen and the region could potentially be in danger.

“Threatening the airspace over the southern Red Sea and turning it into a danger zone for civilian aircraft and passengers represents an escalation that goes beyond the scope of Yemeni airspace safety alone,” he said.

Al-Nazili also said “this dangerous escalation coincides with the threats” by Iranian officials, including Mohsen Rezaei, the secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, to target aviation services in the region after the US sanctioned Iranian airlines .

Rezaei had initially warned that regional airports could lose flights if they joined US restrictions on Iranian aviation. Two days later, his office later clarified that Tehran was not planning military retaliation over the restrictions although it said nonmilitary countermeasures against specific airports remained possible.

Using “Iranian weapons from Yemeni territory poses a direct threat to international air navigation routes and cannot be considered a purely domestic Yemeni issue,” al-Nazili said, calling on international authorities to take “urgent and decisive action”.

Have the Houthis modified Iranian weapons systems?

Eleonora Ardemagni, a senior associate research fellow at the Italian Institute for International Political Studies, told Al Jazeera that while there is no conclusive evidence that the Houthis have modified an Iranian air defence system, “a series of things suggest this can’t be ruled out.”

“The Houthis have often demonstrated to be able to innovate despite the warfighting scenario, so the evolution of threat capabilities is a constant for the group,” she said.

Ardemagni said years of research have established that “the Houthis don’t receive assembled missiles from Iran but Iranian-origin components to be assembled, so they have significant expertise in assembling weapons.”

She referred to an incident in June 2025 when the Yemeni government-aligned National Resistance Forces, led by Tareq Saleh, seized a 750-tonne shipment of weapons and military equipment bound for the Houthis, including hundreds of advanced cruise, antiship and anti-aircraft missiles, according to the US military’s Central Command.

In July this year, several media reports, including from the Reuters news agency , said an Iranian Mahan Air flight directed to Yemen’s Houthi-held capital, Sanaa, was carrying IRGC commanders, military advisers and weapons. Al Jazeera could not independently verify this report. “The flight was forced to land in Houthi-controlled Hodeidah at last, the same governorate from which the Yemeni government now states the Houthis would launch cruise missiles,” Ardemagni told Al Jazeera.

Brigadier General Mohammed Al-Kumaim, a Yemeni military and strategic analyst, said the Houthis are no longer content with using Iranian ballistic missiles and drones but have begun employing advanced air defence technologies based on “loitering” cruise missiles.

Al-Kumaim noted that these missiles can remain in the air for up to 25 minutes, tracking the flight path of targets from their electrothermal emissions.

Yemeni military and strategic expert Ali Al-Dhahab told Al Jazeera that the effect of these loitering munition projectiles is to create a “permanent threat” to any moving object in the air, which could temporarily restrict military air movements.

AI giant Anthropic has also identified a weapons-development cell in northern Yemen reportedly linked to the Houthis that used its Claude AI to develop guidance, navigation and control software for a guided rocket and several missile programmes.

What are the Houthis’ known missile capabilities?

The Houthis have a multilayered missile force, ranging from short- and medium-range ballistic missiles to antiship cruise missiles and modified surface-to-air missiles.

Research into the armed group’s arsenal suggested it has evolved substantially from the inherited Yemeni military stockpiles it seized when it took Sanaa in 2014, including Soviet- and Chinese-designed missiles, and has incorporated Iranian-designed missiles.

Here is what we know the Houthis have in their missile arsenal, based on their recent statements:

Palestine-2: a two-stage, solid-fuel missile unveiled by the group that the Houthis claim is hypersonic with a range exceeding 2,000km (1,245 miles)

Toufan: one of their long-range systems, said to have an estimated range of 1,350km to 1,950km (840 to 1,210 miles). An International Institute for Strategic Studies (IISS) assessment said the Toufan appeared to be a rebranded Iranian Ghadr.

Burkan series: short- to medium-range ballistic missiles based on Iranian designs

Quds series: cruise missiles cited by Houthi spokespeople after strikes on oil and economic facilities in the region

Older inventory: The Houthis have historically possessed or modified older variants of missiles that include the Scud-B/-C, Tochka and Qaher-1 ballistic missiles as well as C-802 antiship cruise missiles.

What does this mean for the Red Sea and the Yemen war?

As far as the regional aviation sector is concerned, Saj Ahmad, chief analyst at StrategicAero Research, told Al Jazeera that “critically, air traffic around Yemen is almost nil, and that reduces the propensity of inadvertent threats to passenger airplanes.”

However, “these same missiles are being launched northwards into Saudi Arabia, where there is commercial traffic,” Ahmad added.

That Houthi threat, therefore, poses “a huge dilemma for the Saudis, who will be very reluctant to close off airspace but equally be mindful of the risks of allowing air traffic through when missiles are inbound”, Ahmad said.

He added that the Houthis have “demonstrated that they can hit targets at distance. The attack near Tel Aviv airport last year is but one example.”

When the Houthis’ arsenal is analysed in the context of the crucial Bab al-Mandeb strait, “any missiles that the Houthis have in their armoury can easily decimate ships at will on a much narrower waterway,” Ahmad said.

Yemeni military strategist Al-Kumaim said the introduction of these supposedly new missiles “adds another capability to the military operations theatre south of the Red Sea” and is part of a broader Iranian strategy to exert pressure on regional airspace and energy supply chains.

Analyst Ardemagni noted that Yemen’s government and Saudi Arabia “have an interest in raising the alarm bell for regional security as much as possible given the current ‘loneliness’, in terms of regional and international allies they are experiencing since the Yemen war has reignited”.

She added that if new cruise missiles are demonstrated, “it would certainly contribute to redesigning Red Sea balances in favour of nonstate armed actors.”

articles.title: Russia accused of sabotage by Estonia after arson at Ukraine supplier
articles.summary: Estonian authorities said that an arson attack on a defense company that provides military vehicles to Ukraine was an act of sabotage commissioned by Russia.
articles.body: Estonian authorities said Tuesday that an arson attack carried out last month on a defense company that provides military vehicles to Ukraine was an act of sabotage commissioned by Russian security services. Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna said that “such actions are absolutely unacceptable” and that Russia’s charge d’affaires in Tallinn was being summoned to his ministry. A fire broke out overnight on Aug. 15 at a building in the Estonian capital used by Milrem Robotics, but was quickly brought under control, the BNS news agency reported. On Aug. 17, two Latvian suspects were detained in neighboring Latvia, and a third followed the next day. The suspects were handed over to Estonia. Milrem has supplied THeMIS unmanned ground vehicles to Ukraine. The Estonian Internal Security Service said that it has concluded that the arson attack “was a deliberate and pre-planned act commissioned by Russian security services.” It said in a statement that “the modus operandi of the Milrem attack is consistent with other acts of sabotage carried out in Europe on behalf of Russia,” adding that it “assesses that the attack is directly attributable to the Russian Federation.” Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said that “such statements are unfounded, ill-considered, absolutely not reflecting the reality, not containing any substantiation whatsoever.” “We cannot take such statements seriously, and we won’t,” Peskov said. Moscow has been widely accused by Western officials of running a campaign of sabotage and disruption with the aim of undermining support for Ukraine and destabilizing European nations. The Associated Press has tracked around 200 incidents of sabotage and malign activity across Europe blamed on Russia since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine on Feb. 24, 2022. That includes organizing plots to set fire to warehouses, launching drones and trying to kill enemies abroad as well as stealing defense technology and carrying out cyberattacks on critical European infrastructure. In a recent case that pointed to an escalation of such activity, Germany blamed Russia for an attempted attack at Leipzig/Halle Airport in early August using a drone laden with explosives. Estonian Prime Minister Kristen Michal wrote on X that “we will not be intimidated.”

articles.title: Nowak killer Vickrum Digwa given leave to appeal against sentence
articles.summary: The Court of Appeal will decide in November whether to reduce or lengthen the 21-year minimum term.
articles.body:
The man who murdered student Henry Nowak is being allowed to appeal against the length of his sentence.

Vickrum Digwa stabbed 18-year-old Henry Nowak to death in Southampton in December 2025. In June, he was jailed for life with a minimum term of 21 years.

He has now been given permission to challenge the length of that sentence at the Court of Appeal on 5 November.

The court will also decide on a referral by the Attorney General's office, which argued the sentence was too lenient.

Digwa has also applied to appeal against his conviction for murder, which will be decided separately.

The 23-year-old was also sentenced for possessing a knife in public, despite claiming in court that the 21cm (8in) blade was being carried as part of his Sikh faith.

After stabbing Nowak, who came from Chafford Hundred in Essex, Digwa lied to police that he was the victim of a racist attack.

The case later sparked protests after police body-worn footage was released showing officers failing to give Nowak first aid and instead handcuffing him as he lay dying, despite him telling officers he could not breathe.

The Independent Office for Police Conduct previously said it was investigating two officers for potential gross misconduct.

Twelve police officers and a police dog were injured during the protests in Southampton on 2 June.

Demonstrators gathered outside the city centre police station before moving to an area near the Digwa family home and the murder scene.

More than 30 people have so far been charged with violent disorder following the incident.

On 15 June, former Solicitor General Ellie Reeves KC referred the case to the Court of Appeal under the Unduly Lenient Sentence scheme.

Sikh leaders have reported a "backlash" and increase in "hate crime" against their community following the case.

articles.title: Questions hang over reopening of crumbling Harlequin Theatre in Redhill
articles.summary: The leader of Reigate council says there could be an "indicative" date in the next couple of months.
articles.body:
A reopening date for an unsafe Surrey theatre is yet to be confirmed, according to the Local Democracy Reporting Service (LDRS).

Harlequin Theatre in Redhill was closed in 2023 after it was found to be riddled with dangerous reinforced autoclaved aerated concrete (Raac).

The earliest hoped-for reopening has been 2028 but the leader of Reigate and Banstead Borough Council (RBBC) has said it depends on how long the operator's fit-out work takes once the building has been made safe.

Early estimates said emergency repairs and modernisation - which have yet to begin - would last six to seven months, but this has now doubled to between 12 and 15 months.

Work had been expected to start in June but has now been pencilled in for November.

RBBC leader Richard Biggs said he was confident the local authority could get an "indicative" reopening date in the next couple of months.

He said: "It will be remiss of us at the moment to actually state an opening time when we do not have the final detail.

"I know that work is moving forward, fast and furious."

Raac was widely used between the 1950s and 1990s as a cheaper alternative to concrete but only lasts about 30 years.

More than 230 schools in England were confirmed to contain the material in 2023.

articles.title: Who is Christa Pike? Woman set for Tennessee's first female execution in 200 years
articles.summary: Christa Pike was 18 when she killed her classmate in a jealous rage and became one of the youngest women sentenced to death in the US.
articles.body: Christa Pike was 18 when she killed her classmate in a jealous rage and became one of the youngest women sentenced to death in the US.Now 50, Pike is scheduled to be executed on Wednesday, in what would be Tennessee’s first execution of a woman in 200 years.Pike and her boyfriend were convicted in the 1995 killing of 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer, who was their classmate at Knoxville Job Corps. Prosecutors said Pike saw Slemmer as a romantic rival and lured her to a secluded area, where she and her boyfriend tortured and killed her.The case drew widespread attention because of the brutality of the killing, the young age of those involved and a satanic symbol carved into Slemmer’s body.Pike has never denied killing Slemmer. But her lawyers and supporters say the death penalty is not appropriate for a crime committed when she was 18, especially given her history of sexual abuse, neglect and untreated mental illness.Slemmer’s mother, however, wants Pike’s execution to go ahead. She has said she has waited decades to see the sentence carried out.Tennessee Gov Bill Lee said on Monday that he would not grant Pike clemency. Her lawyers have asked the US Supreme Court to stop the execution.Lawyers point to Pike’s troubled childhoodPike’s lawyers say she suffered severe abuse as a child.Assistant federal defender Stephen Ferrell said Pike was sexually abused from the time she was a toddler and was raped at ages 11 and 17.He said her lawyers during the original trial did not give the jury enough information about her childhood or explain how her age should be considered.Pike was later diagnosed with bipolar disorder and post-traumatic stress disorder.Pike told police that she initially wanted only to fight Slemmer but ended up killing her in a violent attack. In her clemency petition, her lawyers said her untreated mental illness and traumatic childhood made it difficult for her to control her actions.“I was a mentally ill 18-year-old kid. It took me numerous years to even realize the gravity of what I’d done. Even more to accept how many lives I affected. I took the life of someone’s child, sister, friend. It sickens me now to think I had the ability to commit such a crime,” Pike said in a statement included in her clemency petition.Ferrell said scientists now know more about how the brain develops during adolescence and argued that Pike’s death sentence is unusual.Pike’s boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, was 17 when the killing took place. He was sentenced to life with the possibility of parole because of his age. He was denied parole last year. A third teenager involved in the case admitted to being an accessory and received probation.Ferrell said other people sentenced to death in Tennessee for crimes committed at age 18 have since had their sentences reduced.The Death Penalty Information Center said 275 people have been executed in the US in the modern death penalty era for crimes committed when they were 18, 19 or 20. However, death sentences for people in that age group have become increasingly rare.“If Christa Pike was tried today, I do not believe a jury that knew about the documented sexual abuse and neglect she experienced as a child would sentence her to death,” Robin M. Maher, executive director of the Death Penalty Information Center, said.Slemmer’s mother wants execution to go aheadSlemmer’s mother, May Martinez, said she still wants Pike’s execution to take place.Speaking by phone from Florida, Martinez said she often thinks about what her daughter went through.“Every time I think about it, I think about Colleen feeling that pain and trying to get up and run,” Martinez said.Martinez said Slemmer volunteered with the Special Olympics, loved roller skating and wanted to work in computers.“She was easygoing. She was a computer geek to begin with. She and my husband would build and tear apart the computers constantly,” Martinez said. “She trusted everybody, and that was her downfall.”Martinez said her daughter called her from Job Corps on the night of the killing, but the call kept dropping because of poor reception. By the time Martinez called back, Slemmer had already left.“Not a day goes by, or a minute goes by that I do not think about Colleen. Holidays are the worst. Colleen’s birthday was last week. She would have been 51,” Martinez said.The killing shocked Knoxville. Prosecutors said Pike attacked Slemmer with a box cutter and beat her with a large piece of asphalt.The case also became linked to fears about Satan worship during the “satanic panic” of the 1980s and 1990s. Shipp later admitted that he carved a pentagram, a star-shaped symbol associated with Satanism, into Slemmer’s body.Female executions are rare in Tennessee and USIf Pike’s execution goes ahead, it would be Tennessee’s first execution of a woman since 1820, according to the Death Penalty Information Center.Executions of women are also rare across the US. Since 1976, 18 women have been executed in the country, accounting for about 1% of all executions, according to the centre.Missouri executed Amber McLaughlin in 2023 for a 2003 killing. McLaughlin, a transgender woman, is believed to be the first transgender woman executed in the US.In 2021, the federal government executed Lisa Montgomery, the first time in nearly 70 years that the US government had executed a female inmate. articles.title: Somerset Booker Prize nominee praises former school teachers
articles.summary: Luke Kennard, who grew up in Chard, is shortlisted for the award for his novel Black Bag.
articles.body:
An author whose latest book has been nominated for the prestigious Booker Prize said childhood boredom inspired his creativity.

Luke Kennard, who grew up in Chard in Somerset, has been shortlisted for Black Bag , which is based on an experiment involving an actor sitting in a bin bag at the back of a lecture hall.

He said, as a child, he had "quite a lot of time to practice" his creative passions.

Kennard also praised his teachers at the town's Holyrood Academy and said: "It just can't be exaggerated how much difference a teacher can make when they find a kid who has a passion for their subjects."

Kennard said growing up in a quiet town had an impact on his "creative impulse".

"You stay in your room playing the clarinet or writing a poem - there's a certain virtue to being a little bit bored sometimes, and just having to amuse yourself."

Kennard attended Holyrood Academy from 1992 to 1999 and studied both GCSE and A-level English Literature.

He added: "It was the teachers that I had who really encouraged my writing- that's quite foundational."

Kennard said the former head of English, Paul Coffman, would read his short stories during break times, and leave him notes and suggestions.

"He was the first person who really got me to take my writing seriously."

Holyrood Academy said it was "thrilled" with Kennard's nomination.

It added his praise of Coffman "is a moving reminder of the lasting impact teachers can have on the lives and achievements of their students".

"This remarkable accomplishment is a testament to Luke's talent, dedication and love of literature.

articles.title: Hero cop stopped synagogue massacre in Canada as Jewish group calls for armed guards
articles.summary: The Yom Kippur attack outside Sons of Jacob Synagogue in Belleville has intensified demands for armed security at Jewish institutions across Canada.
articles.body: When a gunman approached a police cruiser outside the Sons of Jacob Synagogue in Belleville, Ontario, during Yom Kippur, approximately two dozen people were praying inside. The armed officer sitting outside was not part of a permanent security system available to every synagogue in Canada. Police had dispatched him after receiving a report about a suspicious vehicle. That decision may have prevented a massacre. "The only thing that stood in the way of every congregant of that shul being murdered was the presence of an armed police officer," Simon Wolle, CEO of B’nai Brith Canada, told Fox News Digital. ISRAELI MEDICS TRAIN US SYNAGOGUES HOW TO RESPOND TO ATTACKS, AS HIGH HOLIDAYS APPROACH Police said last week's shooting was a deliberate, hate-motivated attack targeting the Jewish community. According to authorities, 29-year-old Sean Ward approached Belleville Police Constable Jeff Smith and allegedly shouted, "You are going to die for the Jews," before firing a shotgun at him. Smith was struck multiple times while still inside his vehicle. Despite his injuries, he emerged from the cruiser and returned fire. A second officer arrived within minutes and joined the confrontation. Ward later died at a hospital. Smith remains hospitalized after suffering multiple gunshot wounds to his head and body and serious head trauma. Belleville Police Chief Murray Rodd said Smith faces multiple surgeries and a "lengthy and challenging" recovery, but said the officer is "making progress every day." Smith’s wife, Ashley, has also spoken publicly about her husband’s recovery, describing the shooting as "the scariest and darkest day of our lives." "My words aren’t strong or steady yet, but I knew I needed to find them," she wrote. "I needed to use my voice for my dear Jeff, until he is able to use his." MAN CHARGED WITH ASSAULT, HATE CRIMES AFTER ALLEGEDLY DISRUPTING SHABBAT SERVICES AT NYC SYNAGOGUE Ashley Smith also addressed the Jewish community directly, thanking those who have supported her husband and their family. "Please know that your love, your prayers and your support have reached us," she wrote. "We are deeply grateful. We love you, we see you, we pray for you." She said her husband still faces "a very long, difficult road ahead," but added that he is surrounded by what she called "an army of love." The worshipers inside the synagogue were not physically injured. Investigators later disclosed that the gunman possessed what Belleville Police Chief Murray Rodd described as the "means, motive and mechanisms to cause a mass casualty and the destruction of the Jewish synagogue." Police also reported discovering combustible materials inside the suspect’s vehicle. "This individual had the means, the intention, the deliberate plans and the capacity to conduct a murderous massacre," Wolle said. For Wolle, the attack exposed more than a violent act of antisemitism. It revealed a legal and security system that he believes leaves Canadian Jewish institutions dangerously vulnerable. B’nai Brith Canada is calling for changes to federal and provincial laws that would allow synagogues, Jewish schools and other vulnerable institutions to hire qualified armed security guards. "There is currently no legislation in place that allows for Jewish institutions to hire the kind of armed protection that may be necessary," Wolle said. Canada’s firearms regulations are controlled at the federal level, while private security is also governed through separate provincial rules. Wolle said those frameworks must be aligned so institutions confronting credible threats have a lawful way to employ trained, licensed armed guards. FLORIDA MAN INDICTED FOR ALLEGEDLY PLOTTING MASS SHOOTING TARGETING JEWISH EMPLOYEES AT ADVOCACY ORGANIZATION At present, he said, Jewish institutions can ask police departments to increase patrols, although departments cannot always guarantee that an officer will be stationed outside. Communities can also try to hire paid-duty police officers, but availability remains limited. "So the only option right now for the Jewish community to protect itself from the unprecedented amount of violent attacks taking place all across this country is to plead with local police services to come by if they can," Wolle said. "They will not guarantee that they will do so in most circumstances." That leaves Jewish communities spending their own money to reinforce buildings, install surveillance systems and hire officers when available. "Right now, the Jewish community is using its own money primarily to build walls, put up stronger fences, add cameras and then pay for the privilege of having an armed police officer," Wolle said. "Our lives are being threatened across the country, and the government hasn’t taken the steps to offer the necessary protection." B’nai Brith has made two requests. It wants laws amended to permit qualified armed private security at vulnerable Jewish institutions, and it wants the government to fund an increased police presence at those locations. Wolle said the burden of protecting Jewish Canadians from targeted violence should not rest solely on the people being threatened. "The government needs to meet its most basic obligation and responsibility, which is to protect its citizens," he said. The numbers provide a stark context for his concerns. Statistics Canada recorded 788 police-reported hate crimes targeting Jewish people in 2025, representing more than 70% of all reported religiously motivated hate crimes that year. Wolle said Jewish Canadians constitute approximately 1% to 2% of the country’s population, yet remain overwhelmingly affected by religiously motivated hate crimes. Preliminary data from B’nai Brith’s 2026 annual audit indicate that violent antisemitic incidents have already more than tripled compared with the total recorded throughout 2025. "There is a national crisis of Jew hatred in Canada," Wolle said. B’nai Brith has been warning for months that antisemitic violence is accelerating. Wolle said the organization submitted recommendations and concrete plans to different levels of government before the Belleville attack. "We’ve been calling for many things from all levels of government," he said. "We provided concrete action plans to each." The shooting has intensified the organization’s demand that lawmakers treat the security of Jewish institutions as an emergency rather than another subject for future discussion. "The most urgent thing that is needed is a mechanism for there to be armed protection of Jewish institutions that are under attack right now in Canada," Wolle said. He emphasized that B’nai Brith is not calling for firearms to be placed indiscriminately inside synagogues and schools. Its proposal concerns trained, vetted and qualified security professionals operating under a clearly defined legal framework. "If we don’t have enough armed officers, then we need legislative frameworks changed to allow for alternative armed guards to protect Jewish institutions," Wolle said. Prime Minister Mark Carney condemned the Belleville attack and called on anyone with information to contact law enforcement. RECORD ANTISEMITIC INCIDENTS IN CANADA FUEL CRITICISM OF CARNEY GOVERNMENT RESPONSE SIGN UP FOR ANTISEMITISM EXPOSED NEWSLETTER "On the holiest night of the Jewish calendar, a shooting took place outside the Sons of Jacob Synagogue in Belleville," Carney said. "Jewish people must be able to worship safely. To live free, open, proud Jewish lives." Wolle welcomes expressions of support and said Canadian Jews now need their government to move beyond statements. "The government gives us words and no action," he added. Belleville offered a disturbing picture of what could have happened without an armed officer outside. The congregants did not know that a man police say was driven by hatred had allegedly arrived with weapons and the capacity to cause mass casualties. One report of a suspicious vehicle led to one officer being placed outside. That officer, Wolle stressed, became the barrier between the gunman and the people praying inside. "In the wake of these harrowing events, Canada’s Jewish community cannot wait any longer for the government to act," he said. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The people inside the synagogue, Sons of Jacob, survived. Wolle’s warning is that Canada cannot depend on chance, a suspicious-vehicle report or the availability of a single officer the next time a Jewish institution is targeted. "This is not a Jewish community problem," he said. "This is a Canadian problem."

articles.title: Wildfires: Are Hampshire, Dorset and the Isle of Wight prepared?
articles.summary: Experts have warned the risk of wildfires could double within the next 50 years.
articles.body:
Wildfires will increasingly become the norm in the South with the risk likely to double within the next 50 years, according to an expert.

Dr Mark Hardiman, an expert in wildfires from the University of Portsmouth, said fires across the region were larger, burned for longer, and came closer to people's homes and roads.

It comes after a record 1,350 wildfires across England and Wales this year , as the Fire Brigades Union warns crews are overstretched and lack the right equipment to meet the challenge.

Dorset and Wiltshire Fire and Rescue Service said it had significant capability to tackle wildfires, while the government said it was investing nearly £100m to improve national resilience.

Fires broke out right across the region during this summer's heatwaves.

The largest of the blazes came in August, when a van fire on the A31 spread to heathland in the New Forest , affecting more than 100 hectares, an area equivalent to about 140 football pitches.

Firefighters were at the scene for two weeks, while the road was closed for nearly a fortnight as National Highways replaced damaged safety barriers and fencing.

A blaze at Headon Warren, near the Needles, burned for five days and needed 80 firefighters at its peak. Fire engines were ferried across the Solent and a helicopter dropped water on areas crews were unable to reach.

In the New Forest, more than 60 firefighters were called to a fire near Ashurst in July, where discarded disposable barbecues were found.

Nationally, figures from the National Fire Chiefs Council show there were 1,350 wildfires in England and Wales in 2026, the highest number on record and more than 1,000 more than in 2024.

Hardiman said wildfires would "increasingly be the norm".

"Over the next 40-50 years, the risk - particularly in places like the South, the Isle of Wight - is probably going to double," he said.

The UK's Climate Change Committee has also warned that the risk could double across much of the UK by 2050.

Antony Bholah, area manager at Dorset and Wiltshire Fire and Rescue Service, said the conditions that allowed fires to start and spread quickly were becoming more frequent.

"We need to recognise that the risk is changing. We need to be more prepared for it," he said.

While hot, dry weather creates the conditions for wildfires, fire services say many still start because of human activity, including barbecues, campfires, discarded cigarettes, farm machinery and deliberate fire-setting.

James Leslie, South West regional secretary of the FBU, said crews had done "remarkably well" but had worked long hours "under really arduous conditions".

He said crews were "more often riding a fire engine with four instead of the safe system of five".

"You're waiting longer for the second fire engine to come, and all that time the fires are getting bigger," he added.

The FBU says one in five firefighter posts across the UK have been cut since 2010.

It says Hampshire and Isle of Wight Fire and Rescue Service has lost one in four of its firefighters over that time, while Dorset and Wiltshire's firefighter numbers have fallen from 1,297 to 981.

Both fire services have been approached for comment on the union's figures.

Hardiman said more resources were needed to cope with several large fires at once.

"If you don't have the resources, you have to start picking and choosing which ones you fight," he said.

Bholah admitted it was "challenging", but said the service planned for it.

He said Dorset's firefighters had worked with neighbouring services to provide help across borders, and could call on national resilience arrangements.

Leslie said most firefighters in the South West, including those in Dorset and Wiltshire, were still using kit designed for structural fires in buildings rather than lightweight equipment made for fighting fires in the open.

Bholah said the service was "quite fortunate" to have four-by-four fire engines and specialist vehicles designed for rough terrain, and was continually reviewing whether it had enough.

Dorset and Wiltshire Fire and Rescue Service has a £500,000 off-road Unimog based at Wareham to reach fires in remote rural locations , while the Hampshire service has a new specialist off-road fire engine based at Rushmoor.

Hardiman said fighting wildfires required different equipment from house fires, because crews had to travel long distances and spend long periods on foot.

He said fire services across the South had been learning from crews in Portugal and Spain about how to tackle larger, more aggressive wildfires.

Hardiman said the solutions for fighting wildfires were already known and tackling the problem came down to a "political choice".

He argued for investment in people as well as equipment, so that "when we do have another year or even a worse year over the next few decades, we are able to fight it and hopefully defend homes".

Leslie called for a national approach, including a consistent definition of what counts as a wildfire, national aerial firefighting capability and nationally recognised training.

Bholah said: "I don't think it's always a case of just throwing money at a problem. I think we need to be really sure about where that money needs to be spent."

The government temporarily banned the sale of disposable barbecues in August, saying they had caused a number of serious wildfires over the summer.

Bholah said the service had been campaigning for the ban and was "really pleased" when it came in, but said more needed to be done to educate the public.

The government said its £97m would fund six specialist firefighting teams to work across the UK, as well as equipment such as off-road vehicles.

The prime minister has also said the government will hold a summit with fire and rescue services to make sure they have the right equipment and resources.

articles.title: Why has Putin added 15,000 new soldiers to Russia’s army?
articles.summary: The move marks the fourth military expansion this year as Russia’s war in Ukraine seemingly stalls.
articles.body:
Russian President Vladimir Putin has ordered another military expansion, adding 15,500 military personnel as Moscow’s battlefield advances in Ukraine have stalled after more than four and a half years of fighting.

Putin signed the decree on Sunday, marking the fourth time this year the president has increased the authorised size of the Russian military. Together, the orders have added 47,860 military personnel since March.

This comes as both sides have increasingly been relying on drones and long-range strikes against each other.

Ukraine, meanwhile, has repeatedly accused Moscow of preparing another mobilisation – something Putin has dismissed as Ukrainian “disinformation”.

So why has Putin issued this decree, and where is the conflict headed?

“The authorised personnel strength of the Russian armed forces is to be set at 2,441,630 units, including 1,550,500 military personnel,” the decree said.

It did not elaborate on why the additional troops were needed or how they would be recruited. Putin had already issued orders expanding the military in March, June and July.

Andrei Kortunov, director general of the Russian International Affairs Council, dubbed the expansion technical.

“This is mostly a technical decision rather than a strategic shift. It is technical in the sense that another 15,000 will not change the conflict dynamics,” he told Al Jazeera.

“As for a diplomatic solution, we are still far away from it.”

Why has Putin decided to increase the size of the army?

The Kremlin has not publicly given a reason, but the order comes as Russia faces mounting human and material losses together with limited territorial gains.

Ukraine expert Olena Halushka says Russia’s war effort is not going according to plan.

“Last year, at the Anchorage summit [in the US state of Alaska], Putin continued to demand that Ukraine withdraw from the rest of the Donetsk region that Russia had failed to capture, likely claiming that Ukraine would soon lose those lands anyway. Yet a year afterwards, the situation on the battlefield today shows absolutely the opposite,” Halushka, a board member at the Anti-Corruption Action Centre in Kyiv, told Al Jazeera.

“Putin’s latest decree is … likely not the last, and should be viewed in the context of Russia’s continuing efforts to expand the manpower available for a protracted war,” she added.

Russia’s advances have slowed sharply this year, with the widespread use of drones making large concentrations and rapid movements of troops increasingly dangerous.

Ukraine’s military said earlier this month that Russian losses in 2026 had surpassed 300,000, and estimated that Moscow suffered more than 20,000 casualties in the first half of September alone. Al Jazeera could not independently verify those figures.

The latest decrees also come as Ukraine repeatedly claims Moscow is looking outside Russia to bolster its forces and is preparing another mobilisation, a claim Russia denies.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on Monday said that more than 8,000 North Korean soldiers were currently in Russia and preparations were under way to deploy another 10,000. North Korea has already sent an estimated 14,000 to 15,000 soldiers to support Russia since 2024, according to Ukrainian and South Korean estimates.

Putin last ordered a mobilisation of reservists in September 2022 after Russia suffered a series of battlefield setbacks.

Nevertheless, Russia expert Alexey D Muraviev said this latest increase was unlikely to be linked to Ukraine.

“Putting things into place would require some time in terms of planning, in terms of recruitment, in terms of formation of new units, and that’s not going to address Russia’s immediate operational needs at the theatre of war,” Muraviev, professor and senior research fellow in Defence and Strategic Studies at Edith Cowan University, told Al Jazeera.

In his view, Putin’s decision to increase the military has more to do with “longer-term strategic considerations” such as Moscow’s tensions with NATO, and the “increased possibility of a major open conflict between Russia and NATO in the foreseeable future”.

“This also drives Russia’s continuous reorganisation of its military, the expansion of its standing force, and the formation of new units, including army divisions and marine divisions.

“We should also be mindful that the Russians are concerned about the buildup of Japan’s military power, as well as US military power in the Pacific, and subsequently the need to respond to those security concerns.”

Russia and Ukraine continue to exchange major aerial attacks even as the ground war moves slowly.

At least 10 people were killed and more than 80 wounded in Russian attacks across the country on Monday.

Russian drones struck the National Academy of Sciences in central Kyiv , while attacks were also reported in Dnipro, Kharkiv, Zaporizhia and other parts of Ukraine.

Russian forces have also increased their attacks on the Ukrainian capital, Kyiv, forcing a top university – Taras Shevchenko National University – to switch to remote classes.

Shevchenko University said it would “switch to a remote format of work” until at least October 16, “due to the deteriorating security situation in Kyiv”.

Meanwhile, Ukraine, on the eastern front, has reportedly been making gains in northern Donetsk. According to the Reuters news agency, a senior Ukrainian commander said Kyiv’s forces had recaptured 51 square kilometres (19.7sq miles) in a recent operation, taking the total recovered during that operation to 176sq km (68sq miles).

Donetsk remains one of the central battlegrounds – and a major sticking point in negotiations – with Ukraine still controlling about 20 percent of the region.

Russia annexed four occupied Ukrainian regions, including Donetsk and Luhansk, in 2022. The move has not been recognised by the international community, including the UN.

What is the latest on the diplomatic front?

While diplomatic efforts have resumed, there has been no breakthrough.

Russia wants Ukraine to cede the eastern region annexed by it and wants Kyiv to renounce its NATO ambitions. But Ukraine has ruled out territorial concessions, and has urged its European allies to provide a security guarantee in case of a deal.

Earlier this month, US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner travelled to Moscow and Kyiv, meeting Putin and Zelenskyy as Washington sought to restart negotiations. Zelenskyy later said the envoys had presented “decent ideas”, although fundamental disagreements remained, particularly over territory.

According to Zelenskyy, Washington is now seeking technical-level trilateral talks involving Russia, Ukraine and the US, with the United Arab Emirates floated as a possible venue.

Putin said last week that proposals to resume negotiations remained “on the table”, while saying his country still needed to assess what was in its best interest.

Ukraine expert Halushka said a diplomatic solution was not possible as long as Moscow concludes that “continuing the war will cost it less than ending it”.

“Russia’s actions suggest that the Kremlin still believes it can improve its position through military force, terrorism against Ukrainian civilians and breaking Western support for Ukraine,” she noted.

“At the same time, Russia is escalating its hybrid activities in Europe, which shows that the security challenge it poses extends well beyond the battlefield in Ukraine.”

According to academic Muraviev, the war in Ukraine has entered “a new escalation phase” as Moscow intensifies its aerial campaign and achieves “air dominance” through drone and missile attacks.

He believes the escalation is a response to the “so-called 40-day special operation which Zelenskyy announced back in June,” aimed at undermining Russia’s war effort and public morale before parliamentary elections.

In turn, Muraviev argues, the Kremlin decided “to demonstrate its capacity to bring Ukraine down to its knees”, systematically destroying key sectors of Ukraine’s economy, from the steel industry to agricultural exports, and imposing a de facto naval blockade without using its Black Sea Fleet.

Muraviev says Russia is now striking data and communication centres, refineries, bridges and locomotives to make the war “simply unaffordable to its Western allies”.

A proposal by US President Donald Trump for an energy truce between the two sides has failed to stop the tit-for-tat attacks.

articles.title: Pine marten kit spotted at Longleat Safari Park in Wiltshire
articles.summary: The pine marten kit was caught on camera at the Longleat estate in Wiltshire.
articles.body:
A rare pine marten kit has been captured on camera in an area where there is no formal re-introduction programme.

Longleat Estate in Wiltshire revealed in February that two of the mammals had been spotted together, bringing hope of a family.

The safari park then made changes to support the animls, including installing den boxes and changing its woodland management.

"It's extremely exciting that all that work has resulted in kits, said Longleat's head of conservation and research, Dr Tom Lewis. "We now know that they are here to stay and we look forward to seeing our population expand further in the future."

The elusive and cat-sized native mammal from the weasel family was once common across the UK, but habitat loss and hunting had pushed them to the brink of extinction by the beginning of the 20th century.

"Wild populations exist in the New Forest and the Forest of Dean – well within dispersal distance," Lewis said.

There have also been re-introductions into western Somerset on Exmoor, where they have bred successfully .

"It is extremely rare for footage like this to be available, as they are seen so infrequently because they are primarily active at night," Lewis continued.

"You can tell it's a kit on the video as it's small and slightly ungainly as it comes down the tree," he added.

Lewis said the species can have "up to five kits" in a "good habitat", suggesting there might be more already at the safari park.

Caroline Longley, conservation lead south at Wiltshire Wildlife Trust, said: "It's really exciting to see the spread of pine martens, especially when there is still so much we have yet to learn about which routes they're taking into Wiltshire from the New Forest and Somerset."

She added: "Having Longleat be a stepping stone in the mosaic of Wiltshire's woodlands, and beyond, provides a really wonderful opportunity to learn about these fascinating creatures and try and understand their population dynamics as they regain their foothold in the UK."

articles.title: Punjabi man stabbed to death in Canada after intervening in racist altercation; sister alleges police delay
articles.summary: A tragic incident in Mississauga, Canada, where Jagjit Singh Sandhu, a Punjabi man, was fatally stabbed after intervening in a racist altercation. His sister raises concerns over police response and media coverage as a woman has been charged with attempted murder.
articles.body: A Punjabi man stabbed in the neck in Mississauga, Canada, has died from his injuries, while a woman has been charged in connection with the attack.The deceased has been identified as Jagjit Singh Sandhu. His sister, Jaspreet Kaur, said the stabbing took place on September 6 outside a shelter on Dundas Street East.According to Kaur, Sandhu intervened when another Punjabi man was allegedly subjected to racist remarks by the boyfriend of a woman staying at the shelter. She said the boyfriend confronted the Indian man and told him to return to his country.Kaur alleged that Sandhu helped the man leave the area, following which an argument broke out between Sandhu and the boyfriend.During the confrontation, a woman allegedly approached Sandhu from behind and stabbed him on the right side of his neck, Kaur said.The injury damaged major blood vessels, causing severe blood loss and cutting off oxygen to his brain. Sandhu was taken to hospital and later declared brain dead, according to his sister.Peel Regional Police did not identify the victim by name in their statement. Police said officers from the 12 Division Criminal Investigations Bureau responded to a stabbing on Dundas Street East at around 5:30pm on September 6 and found an adult male with a serious stab wound to the neck.The man was taken to hospital in critical condition, police said.Investigators initially arrested a man who had been involved in an altercation with the victim. Police later determined that he was not responsible for the stabbing and released him.Police subsequently identified an adult woman as the suspected attacker, police said. She had fled the area on foot before officers arrived.On September 7, police located 42-year-old Lorena Sanchez of Mississauga, arrested her and charged her with attempted murder. She was held in custody pending a bail hearing at the Ontario Court of Justice in Brampton.Kaur has questioned the handling of the case, alleging that police did not contact the family for three days after the incident and that repeated calls from relatives went unanswered.She also alleged that the incident and Sandhu’s identity were not adequately reported in the media.Kaur said the incident has raised concerns about the safety of Indian and Punjabi youngsters in Canada. articles.title: Meet Dani McTague, the 16-year-old who turned a childhood art project into a lifeline for children in hospitals, delivering over 3,700 art bags
articles.summary: Sixteen-year-old Dani McTague has spent several years turning her love of art into a way to help others.
articles.body: Sixteen-year-old Dani McTague has spent several years turning her love of art into a way to help others. She began ‘Dani’s Dream - Sharing the Love of Art’ in 2020, when she was 10, and schools were closed during the COVID-19 pandemic. After noticing that some children did not have access to art supplies, she set out to share them with those in need.As per Points of Light, the project began with a Facebook page and donations from across the country before growing into an effort that provides art supplies to children’s hospitals, hospice centres, homeless shelters and families in need. Since then, McTague has donated more than 3,700 art bags across three states and created a mobile art cart for OU Children’s Hospital, where supplies are taken directly to paediatric patients.How Dani’s Dream grew from a childhood idea into a nationwide service projectDani McTague said, “I realized not everybody had access to art supplies because schools were closed. I created a Facebook page and a project video explaining what I wanted to do, and donations started arriving from across the country.” Donations soon began arriving from across the country, helping the project grow beyond its original goal.Since then, McTague has distributed more than 3,700 art bags filled with creative supplies to children, hospital patients, seniors, veterans, and others in need. Through grants, donations, and community partnerships, Dani’s Dream has generated more than $30,000 in support, as reported by Oklahoma State University. McTague has also taught workshops as part of the project and said she enjoys seeing children become excited after completing their art projects.Her 4-H work grows through workshops, leadership and mentoringMcTague’s work has extended beyond Dani’s Dream. She has served as a state 4-H Ambassador since age 13 and serves on the State 4-H Leadership Council. She has also led more than 125 workshops across Oklahoma. Her efforts have earned several state and national honors.Oklahoma State University reported that these include the National 4-H Lead to Change Grant, the Prudential Spirit of Community Award, and the President’s Volunteer Service Award at the bronze level. Through her service projects, workshops, and outreach efforts, McTague has impacted more than 135,000 people and logged more than 5,500 volunteer hours. Her service has also included mentoring younger leaders.Oklahoma County 4-H educator Serena Woodard said, “We had an 11-year-old member who wanted to start his own service project, and Dani stepped into a mentor role and helped guide him through planning and carrying it out.”Her Hall of Fame selection comes as a surprise during a family tripMcTague learned about her Hall of Fame selection while she was travelling with her family. She said she was at the airport on her way to Hawaii and was on a plane when Cathleen Taylor, Oklahoma 4-H youth development specialist, called her. After she got off the plane, McTague saw notifications and called Taylor while she was with family.“I was at the airport on my way to Hawaii, and I was on a plane when Cathleen called me.”“When I got off, I had all these notifications. I called her back, and I was with all my family. It was really exciting because it’s been a goal of mine since seventh grade.”McTague was honoured during the Masonic Charity Foundation of Oklahoma Honor Night assembly at the 105th State 4-H Roundup at Oklahoma State University. As a Hall of Fame inductee, she received a $7,500 scholarship sponsored by Farm Credit Associations of Oklahoma.How does Dani McTague plan to help younger 4-H membersMcTague plans to continue expanding Dani’s Dream and serving Oklahoma 4-H during her senior year. She said, “I hope that I can be a mentor to younger 4-H’ers so they can start their own service projects and make an impact on their communities”Oklahoma County 4-H educator Cody Yount said McTague’s work ethic and determination helped distinguish her for the Hall of Fame. He also pointed to her attention to detail and self-motivation. Serena Woodard highlighted McTague’s willingness to help others succeed. articles.title: Men who claim they experienced hell reveal terrifying encounters with demons and the afterlife
articles.summary: Three men describe terrifying visions of hell, demons and the afterlife in an exclusive conversation with Sean Hannity about their experiences.
articles.body: Three men who say they visited hell are sharing chilling accounts of what they believe they encountered, sitting down with Fox News host Sean Hannity to describe their terrifying experiences with the afterlife. "I had no idea how I got there, why. Nothing was explained until the way back," said Bill Wiese, author of "23 Minutes in Hell," on Tuesday's episode of the "Hang Out with Sean Hannity" podcast. "But I was in this actual dungeon, and there were demons in this cell, reptilish in appearance, bumps and scales all over the one's body, huge jaw, sunken in eyes, claws about a foot long. And these particular two are about 12 or 13 feet tall," he recalled. COLTON BURPO DESCRIBES MEETING JESUS AND HEARING ANGELS SING DURING NEAR-DEATH EXPERIENCE Wiese joined pilot Jim Woodford, author of "Heaven, an Unexpected Journey," and former Buddhist monk Steve Kang, now a pastor and author of "Eight Hours in Hell," for an exclusive conversation with Hannity about their accounts of the afterlife. Wiese said he experienced a vision. "I got up at three o'clock in the morning to get a glass of water and, suddenly, I was pulled out of my body... and I found myself falling through the air down this long tunnel, and I was getting hotter and hotter, and I landed on an actual stone floor in a prison cell in hell... a dungeon..." he said. "I never asked for this. I've never gone to dark movies. I have never drank. I've never taken drugs, and I had never had a vision before." After the experience, Wiese said he consulted Scripture, eager to learn whether it described what he said he had seen. FATHER CARLOS MARTINS RECOUNTS CHILLING EXORCISM, CLAIMS WOMAN MOVED OBJECTS WITHOUT TOUCHING THEM "It doesn't matter if people believe my experience. I'm just a signpost to point them to the scriptures and by those be persuaded," he said. "There's 132 verses in the Bible about hell. Jesus mentioned hell [in] 46 different verses, and because it's a message of warning. He's letting people know there really is a hell, and it's far worse than our minds can even conceive." Woodford said his experience began after he took more than the prescribed amount of pain medication he was using to manage severe pain from Guillain-Barré syndrome. He said his previous ambivalence toward faith changed dramatically. Woodford said he believed he was dying inside his truck one evening and called out for God's forgiveness, which he later credited with helping lead to his survival. Woodford recalled being above his truck and traveling through what he described as a tunnel of light before arriving at a place of extraordinary beauty. He said he then approached a chasm where he encountered a towering creature that appeared to emerge from what he believed was hell. "It knew me," Woodford said of an alleged demon. "It said my name. ‘Jim, Jim, this is your time with us. Come to us, Jim. We have been waiting.’" Terrified, Woodford said he cried out three words: "God help me." SITE WHERE JESUS WAS CRUCIFIED AND BURIED REVEALS NEW EVIDENCE THAT BACKS BIBLICAL ACCOUNT Woodford said Jesus spoke to him and told him to "go back" before he eventually regained consciousness in a hospital. Kang's story was different still. The former Buddhist monk was 19 when, after using marijuana that he said was laced with heroin, cocaine and PCP, he attempted suicide and underwent an eight-hour operation. Kang said he experienced what felt like an eternity in hell. "Anything is better on earth," Kang said. "Any suffering on earth is better than the pain I felt in hell." Kang said he awoke after the ordeal surrounded by Christian prayer warriors who had come to pray for him. He later converted to Christianity, became a pastor and said he has devoted his life to sharing his faith. Though Wiese, Woodford and Kang described different circumstances surrounding their experiences, all three said they came away believing they had been given another chance at life for a reason and felt a responsibility to tell others about what they believe lies beyond. articles.title: Russian nuclear-capable bomber plane crashes, killing six people
articles.summary: Tu-95 plane crashed during training flight in uninhabited area of Amur region, Defence Ministry says.
articles.body:
A Russian military aircraft has crashed in the eastern region of Amur, killing at least six crew members and leaving one hospitalised, according to Russia’s Ministry of Defence.

Russian state media on Tuesday cited the ministry as saying the Tu-95 plane crashed during a training flight in an uninhabited area of Amur, a region bordering China.

The plane was flying without ammunition, according to the TASS state-run news agency.

Interfax news agency quoted Russia’s military as saying that an Aerospace Forces commission had been dispatched “to the crash site to establish all the circumstances of the incident”.

Unverified social media videos of the purported crash aftermath showed large amounts of smoke rising from the burning aircraft.

The Tupolev Tu-95 is a large, Soviet-era bomber aircraft that can carry, launch and deliver nuclear weapons.

It was first flown in 1952 but was only introduced into service in 1956 and remains in use, often by the Russian military in routine military exercises.

This is not the first time aircraft have gone down in Russia’s Far East. In July last year, an Antonov An-24 plane crashed in poor weather conditions on its way to the town of Tynda, killing all 48 people on board.

In August 2021, a Mil Mi-8 crashed in the Kamchatka Peninsula of Russia with 16 people on board, most of whom were tourists.

articles.title: Five takeaways from Andy Burnham's Labour conference speech
articles.summary: Big policy announcements and emotional moments as the prime minister delivers a speech to Labour's conference.
articles.body:
Andy Burnham has delivered his first speech to the Labour conference as party leader and prime minister. Here is what stood out.

It was no surprise to see Andy Burnham tieless and roaming the conference stage in Liverpool, unanchored by the traditional leader's speech podium.

But despite the relaxed TED talk vibe, this was sober and serious speech. He set out major new policies - not always a given on these occasions - and spoke with real emotion about his family and working class roots.

There were few jokes - and in stark contrast to his predecessor Sir Keir Starmer's speech last year, he did not mention Nigel Farage or Kemi Badenoch once.

But he also avoided mention of some of the trickier issues he faces, such as welfare reform and how his government will pay for promised increases in defence spending.

Follow live: Reaction and analysis of Burnham's speech

Much of his speech was aimed at the party faithful, with a promise to "break with the direction of the past 40 years and put Britain on a new path", and bring back traditional Labour values.

It went down extremely well in the hall. We counted 11 standing ovations in just over an hour.

The first came when he vowed to overturn Margaret Thatcher's 1980s reforms to give the public greater control over housing, water and energy.

The new part was a plan to legislate later this year to repeal Thatcher's "ideological ban on public ownership of water companies".

He said this would put the UK on a 10-year path to a "very different water system" - although there was not an explicit commitment to renationalisation.

The run up to the speech was dominated by speculation about whether Burnham would scrap the state pension triple lock, which guarantees increases in line with the highest of inflation, earnings or 2.5%.

In the end, it was a bit more nuanced than that.

He said he would "honour" Labour's commitment to keep the triple lock until the end of the current Parliament.

But from April 2030, the state pension would rise every year by inflation or 2.5%, whichever is higher, under Burnham's plans - and it will be increased in some years if needed to keep pace with average worker earnings.

The change, he said, would "generate significant savings" to fund his long-held ambition of creating a National Care Service in England.

"I accept I may pay a political price," he told the conference.

"But someone has to go through the pain barrier and rip the plaster off."

4. Electoral reform cheered by conference

Burnham has made no secret of his desire to scrap Westminster's first-past-the-post voting system.

And his announcement of a national commission on electoral reform went down very well with many in the hall, who have been calling for it.

"We will contest the next election with a manifesto commitment to change the electoral system so that everyone's vote counts and everyone's voice is heard," he said to cheers.

As he neared the end of his speech, Burnham appeared overcome by emotion and it looked for a brief moment as though he could not carry on.

He was speaking about his father Roy, who he lost to Alzheimer's earlier this month.

"If only, if only he had been able to appreciate that moment of the family in Downing Street," Burnham said of his first day in his new role.

"The son of a man who failed his 11-plus becoming prime minister."

The longest ovation of all came when he pledged to "use this job to build the kind of Britain my dad wanted to see – and fight with everything I've got to keep it together".
